bio.en: Fiona Fung leads the teams behind Claude Code and Cowork at Anthropic, and is a 25-year engineering veteran who previously built TypeScript and Visual Studio at Microsoft and founded Facebook Marketplace, which now drives over $100 billion in GMV a year.
bio.zh: Fiona Fung 在 Anthropic 领导 Claude Code 和 Cowork 背后的团队，是一位拥有 25 年经验的工程老将，此前在微软打造了 TypeScript 和 Visual Studio，并在 Facebook 创立了如今年 GMV 超 1000 亿美元的 Facebook Marketplace。

summary.en: Fiona describes how AI has removed coding as the bottleneck—Anthropic engineers now ship roughly 8x the code per quarter versus 2025—so the constraint is ambition, not ability. She explains that the people thriving are those with the most agency and initiative, paired with accountability, and argues teams should 'lean in' to fear rather than resist it. We also hear about the emerging gap between AI-native and AI-resistant engineers, the loneliness risk of agent-only work (and their 'pair-wise programming lunch'), and what long-time engineering leaders should be thinking about right now.
summary.zh: Fiona 描述了 AI 如何消除了编码这一瓶颈——Anthropic 工程师如今每季度提交的代码量约为 2025 年的 8 倍——所以限制因素变成了“野心”而非“能力”。她解释道，表现最好的人是那些最具主动性、最有能动性、同时又能承担责任的人，并主张团队应“迎难而上”面对恐惧而非抗拒。我们还听到 AI 原生工程师与抗拒 AI 的工程师之间正在拉开的差距、纯靠智能体工作的孤独风险（以及他们的“结对编程午餐”），以及资深工程领导者当下应当思考什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Anthropic engineers on average have eight times as much code per quarter as they did compared to 2025.
turns.zh: Anthropic 的工程师，平均每季度写的代码量，是 2025 年时的八倍。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Coding is no longer the bottleneck. It's looked at the ceiling of what anyone is able to do.
turns.zh: 写代码不再是瓶颈。它已经顶到了任何人能做到的上限。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Everything is now possible, in theory. Now it's about how ambitious can you be.
turns.zh: 理论上，现在一切皆有可能。现在的问题是你敢有多大的雄心。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: It's always something we ask ourselves, what's better than me doing it? Having Claude do it.
turns.zh: 我们总问自己一个问题：有什么比我自己做更好？答案是让 Claude 来做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The people that seem to be doing best are taking the most initiative, getting the most proactive, have the most agency.
turns.zh: 那些看起来做得最好的人，是主动性最强、最主动出击、最有 agent（自主能动性）的人。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: We say with high agency is also high accountability. So it's all about making sure folks have that freedom to cook. But then it's also like, okay, what's the accountability for it? What's the hypothesis of what you're trying to solve?
turns.zh: 我们说，高自主也意味着高问责。所以关键就是确保大家有那种「放手去搞」的自由。但另一方面也要问：那对应的问责是什么？你想解决的假设是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm curious what is lost in this new world of software engineering.
turns.zh: 我很好奇，在这个软件工程的新世界里，有什么东西消失了。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: It could start being a lonely experience because we all started just working with our agents so much. And on the Claude Code team recently we started a para-wise programming lunch.
turns.zh: 它可能会开始变成一种孤独的体验，因为我们大家都越来越多地只跟自己的 agent 一起工作。最近在 Claude Code 团队，我们发起了一个「pair-wise programming lunch（结对编程午餐）」。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something you think about is this gap forming between people that are leaning into AI, killing it, and then people that are not, super frustrated, fighting, resisting.
turns.zh: 你会想到这样一种正在形成的鸿沟：一边是全力拥抱 AI、杀疯了的人，另一边是不拥抱、超级沮丧、在对抗、在抗拒的人。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: In terms of frustration, I think sometimes I also see a little bit of fear. For anything that there is a fear, my advice is lean in and ask, " What can I do about it? What is within my control?"
turns.zh: 说到沮丧，我想我有时也会看到一点点恐惧。对任何让人恐惧的事，我的建议是迎上去，然后问：「我能为此做点什么？什么是我能控制的？」

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung

turns.zh: 而最离谱的是，仅仅过去两年，工程师这个工作就变了这么多。简直是份完全不同的工作。大家可能忘了，不久之前 100% 的代码都是人写的，而现在正在走向 100% 的代码由 AI 写。就像 Boris 那句名言：编码已经被解决了。顺着这个方向，你们昨天发了条 tweet，展示了——这是那条 tweet：「Anthropic 工程师平均每季度写的代码量，是 2021 到 2025 年期间的八倍。」我们会在屏幕上放出这张图。它就是稳、稳、稳、稳，然后直接射向月球。(00:03:45)：所以这个角色变化得有多离谱。我很好奇，你作为一个亲历其中的工程师，走了这么长的路，在早期做了很久工程师，这一路上有哪几个大的节点，改变了你的思维和运作方式，最终把你带到了你现在做的事、以及你现在的运作方式？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Oh, I love this kind of love walk back in time. Yeah. IBM, working on DB2, the operating system services team. Back then I was thinking, "Oh, what's a hard area of the stack?" And I really thought the lower level you go closer to the OS, then it's more hardcore and you'll learn more. So I was really fortunate to gone into the IBM internship. But the funny thing was, I think there's even a big shift from IBM to Microsoft. So at IBM it was I think VIM. I didn't have an IDE that we used. I think there might have been an Eclipse license, but for some reasons, most of us didn't use it. (00:04:40): So I remembered it was mainly like VIM and kind of terminal debugging. And then when I joined Microsoft, I mean, this is how naive I was, I didn't even know about IDEs and such. And back then you didn't really get to pick teams. His was early 2000s. Actually, first off, I should say I was so grateful that I landed the internship and the role, because to take us all the way back in time, the dot com bubble burst in 2000. And so for my graduating class, a lot of the companies weren't hiring or were hiring freezes. So I was so fortunate when Microsoft extended me an offer. (00:05:14): And so they're like, "You're going to work on Visual Studio." I did not even know what Visual Studio was because I came from a Unix school. So I remembered asking, because I was thinking, well, the name Visual Studio, I'm like, "Oh, is this a better Paint program?" And I could tell the look of my manager's face like, "What is going on?" But then it ended up becoming the love of my life for the first 11 years of my career. But that was the first time I used an IDE. So joining the Visual Studio team seeing, "Oh wow, here's an IDE with debuggers and you can set break points and do multi-threaded debugging." (00:05:47): That was also always mind-blowing for me to think about the stepwise change. So yeah, that was kind of the story going from IBM to Visual Studio. And then what I really loved actually about Visual Studio is I was on the Visual Studio editor team. So I used a VS editor to build the VS editor and that's where my whole love of dog fitting comes from. I remembered I wanted to first and foremost create a delightful experience, not only for myself, but for my teammates, because also if we go back in that time, if you remember, I mean, when did Twitter come out? Was it 2006 or so?
turns.zh: 我太爱这种「时光倒流」式的聊天了。对。IBM，在 DB2、操作系统服务团队。那时候我在想：「哦，技术栈里哪块最难？」我真的以为，你越往底层、越靠近 OS，就越 hardcore、学到越多。所以能进 IBM 实习我特别幸运。但有趣的是，我想从 IBM 到微软之间就有一次大转变。在 IBM 时我们用的好像是 VIM，没有真正用 IDE。可能有个 Eclipse 授权，但出于某些原因我们大多数人没用。(00:04:40)：所以我记得主要就是 VIM 加终端调试。而当我加入微软时——可见我当时多 naive——我连 IDE 是什么都不知道。而且那是 early 2000s，你其实不能自己挑团队。首先我得说，我能拿到那个实习和职位我无比感恩，因为把时间拉回更早，2000 年互联网泡沫破了。所以对我那一届毕业生来说，很多公司不招人，或者冻结招聘。所以微软给我发 offer 时我太幸运了。(00:05:14)：然后他们说：「你要去做 Visual Studio。」我甚至不知道 Visual Studio 是什么，因为我来自 Unix 体系。所以我记得我问了，因为我在想，名字叫 Visual Studio，我就想：「哦，这是个更好的画图程序吗？」我能看出我经理脸上的表情，像在说「这什么情况？」但它最后成了我职业生涯头 11 年的最爱。但那是我第一次用 IDE。所以加入 Visual Studio 团队看到「哦哇，这是个带调试器的 IDE，你能设断点、做多线程调试」。(00:05:47)：那一步式的改变对我而言也总是让人 mind-blowing。 对，那就是从 IBM 到 Visual Studio 的故事。而关于 Visual Studio 我真正爱的其实是：我当时在 Visual Studio 编辑器团队。所以我是用 VS 编辑器来构建 VS 编辑器本身的——我对 dogfooding（自家人用自己的产品）的全部热爱就源于此。我记得我最想做的，是首先创造出一种令人愉悦的体验，不只为自己，也为我的队友，因为回到那个年代，如果你记得的话——Twitter 是啥时候出的？大概 2006 年左右？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like it's been around my whole life.
turns.zh: 感觉它好像在我整个人生里都在。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: But back then, before social media, it was also harder for most engineers to hear fast customer feedback. For sure, there you would be user research sessions or we would have customers visit us. But you didn't get the rapid feedback that you do nowadays. But back then I was so lucky because I was on VS. We ourselves gave each other so much rapid feedback because we were all heavy VS users on the team.
turns.zh: 但那时候，在社交媒体出现之前，大多数工程师要快速听到客户反馈也更难。当然，那时会有用户研究环节，或者让客户来拜访我们。但你拿不到今天这种快速反馈。不过当时我特别幸运，因为我在 VS。我们彼此之间给了对方极快的反馈，因为我们团队里所有人都是重度 VS 用户。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yeah. When I worked on Visual Studio, back then we also shipped software on CDs.
turns.zh: 对。我在做 Visual Studio 时，那时候我们还是把软件刻在 CD 上发的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I remember that.
turns.zh: 我记得那个。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: And that's why they were really hard deadlines because you had to make sure the software was ready for us to give to manufacturing, to then put on the CDs for us to then put on the shelves. turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe just kind of set this theme that I want to have for this conversation. A lot of people are just wondering what is software engineering, managing software engineers, managing software and product teams look like in the future? And you are living through that right now. So you mentioned this point about a more focus on verification, making sure the quality of the code being 8X is actually high and something that will work. So just like let me ask this broad question, let's kind of see where this conversation goes. What does an AI pilled software team look like in 2026?
turns.zh: 也许就借这个，定一下我想让这场对话贯穿的主题。很多人都在想：未来的软件工程、管理软件工程师、管理软件和产品团队，会是什么样？而你此刻正在亲历这一切。你刚提到了更聚焦「验证」这一点——确保那 8 倍代码的质量确实高、确实能 work。所以我就问这个宽泛的问题，看看对话往哪走。一个被 AI 武装的软件团队，在 2026 年长什么样？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Because the roles are blowing, it's shifting more to this builder. Everybody starts being a builder, I would say. The other shift that I've recently done is I actually have a Claude Code remote session that I enlist in all of our repos. And so this way I have full visibility into the work that everybody's doing. And this instance, it also has access to all our Slack channels and I'll have access to how are the metrics of everything we track. And so every month when I'd be like, "Hey, you know what's fun? Let's take a look back." (00:10:36): And so we'll actually do it together. I'll share my Claude Code, I've shared my screen, then we do our Claude Code session and it's just about, "Hey, what were the focus areas? What were some of the products that got shipped? How did it do? Oh, what were the feedback channels?" And so even though before I would've just used these sessions to generate PRs and bug fixes, I actually have these sessions to enable me to have conversations with folks that I support.
turns.zh: 因为角色在被打破，它更多转向了「builder（构建者）」。我会说，每个人都在成为 builder。我最近做的另一个转变是：我其实在我们的所有 repo 里都挂了一个 Claude Code 远程 session。这样我对所有人正在做的工作就有完全的可见性。而且这个实例还能访问我们所有 Slack 频道，我也能看到我们追踪的各项指标。所以每个月我会说：「嘿，知道什么好玩吗？咱们回头看看。」(00:10:36)：然后我们就一起做。我会共享我的 Claude Code、共享我的屏幕，然后我们一起跑我们的 Claude Code session，就聊：「嘿，当时的焦点是哪些？都发了哪些产品？效果怎么样？哦，反馈渠道有哪些？」所以即便以前我用这些 session 只是生成 PR 和修 bug，现在我其实是用这些 session 来让我能跟我所支持的人对话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Say more about that. So this is a management technique, let's say, to help people not just ship but actually ship better, understand if they're shipping things that have impact. Is that kind of the idea here? Just use Claude to keep on top of all the things people are shipping and then make that a conversation with them?
turns.zh: 再多讲讲。所以这是一种管理技巧，比如说，帮大家不只是把东西发出去，而是真的发得更好、搞明白他们发的是不是有影响力。是这个意思吗？就是把 Claude 用来持续掌握所有人发货的情况，然后把它变成跟他们的一次对话？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Exactly. So yeah, outside of just the action of shipping is how did it do in market or, hey, did we caught some bugs? And it's okay to, I have this saying, make new mistakes. It's okay to make mistakes, just make new ones so that we're always learning. Because if you aim to make zero mistakes, that probably means you're not moving fast enough or being a little bit too cautious. (00:11:42): And so by having Claude, so then it can also look at, for example, actually, I was just looking at, oh, given some of the incidents that we have, let's look across all of this. Can we generate a theme? What's a good area investment for us next, especially we think about quality. Are we seeing any hotspots of where there could be a gap? I think that used to be just a much more manual process, I would say. If I look back a year ago, I don't think I would've been able to have some of these insights with Claude.
turns.zh: 没错。所以是的，除了「发货」这个动作本身，还有它在市场上表现如何、嘿我们有没有抓到一些 bug？而且——我有句话叫「make new mistakes（犯新的错）」。犯错没关系，只要犯的是新的错，这样我们就在一直学。因为如果你目标是零错误，那大概率说明你动得不够快、或者太谨慎了。(00:11:42)：而有了 Claude，它也能去看，比如我刚在看：鉴于我们遇到的一些事故，咱们把所有这些都拉通看。我们能归纳出个主题吗？下一步我们该在哪块投资，尤其当我们思考质量时？我们是不是看到某些可能有 gap 的热点？我想那过去是个更手动的过程。如果我回看一年前，我觉得我不可能用 Claude 拿到这些洞察里的某些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Well, partly it's because there's that and also people weren't shipping as much so you could just make a little bullet list. Here's the things I shipped last quarter, this feature, that feature, this feature, that feature.
turns.zh: 对。嗯，部分原因是那时有这个、而且人们也没发那么多，所以你只要列个小 bullet list 就行。这是我上季度发的：这个功能、那个功能、这个功能、那个功能。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, I think what I'm hearing here is this is one of the only ways to stay on top of all the things a teammate is shipping. So this is a really cool thread of just how you found ways to stay on top of this 8X increase in code. What else has worked in helping you and your team stay on top of and maintain quality of all the stuff that y'all are shipping because that's obviously a challenge, a bigger challenge.
turns.zh: 所以我想我听到的是：这是保持掌握一个队友在发什么货的唯一几种方式之一。所以这是一个很酷的线索——你是怎么找到办法，跟上这 8 倍代码增长的。还有什么办法帮到你和你的团队，跟上、并维持你们所有人发出的东西的质量？因为那显然、而且越来越大，是个挑战。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yeah. And so definitely the feedback channels are really important to us, but then we also get a lot of feedback. And for example, even I myself, usually my morning ritual would be I get my morning cup of coffee and then I look at the feedback channels and then I try to pick, oh, if I have some maker time, what's something that maybe I would be able to help out or what I could see some gaps like that. It just used to be something I would do every morning. And yeah, I think maybe a month or two ago we launched Routines and that's also completely changed. (00:13:11): Now I just have a routine that automates all this for me. And then there's also, it's almost like before I would be able to generate some prompts, but now with Routines, it's almost like I'm having an agent help me generate the prompts and the PR. So for example, one is, "Hey, keep a look on this feedback channel, what are some of the themes?" And then when I wake up, then I have a really good summary of that and then even some PRs that I'll be able to take a look and review.
turns.zh: 对。所以反馈渠道对我们真的很重要，但我们收到的反馈也很多。比如就连我自己，通常我的晨间仪式是：端起早上的那杯咖啡，然后看看反馈渠道，然后我试着挑——哦，如果我有段 maker time，有什么是我能帮上忙的，或者我能看出些什么 gap 的。那本来是我每天早晨会做的事。而对的，我想大概一两个月前我们上线了 Routines（例程），它彻底改变了这个。(00:13:11)：现在我只是有个 routine 自动帮我把这一切做了。而且——以前我还能生成一些 prompts，但现在有了 Routines，几乎就像是有个 agent 在帮我生成 prompts 和 PR。比如其中一个是：「嘿，盯着这个反馈渠道，有什么主题？」然后我醒来时，就有一份特别好的总结，甚至还有一些 PR 我能看一眼、审一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the feedback channel, where's that feedback coming from? Is that like emails, Twitter, or a combo of everything?
turns.zh: 那反馈渠道，这些反馈是从哪来的？是邮件、Twitter，还是什么组合？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Our feedback channels are definitely like we have a lot from internal ends, but also emails, channels. Actually everybody when we all get feedback on either when friend's ping us or on LinkedIn or socials, we'll all actually post all of that in Slack as well. And we also have of course partnerships and so we have different channels for all the various sources, but that's what I mean. I need Claude's help to help me stay on top because there is so much incoming feedback.
turns.zh: 我们的反馈渠道当然有非常多来自内部，但也有邮件、各种频道。其实任何人——当我们在朋友 ping 我们、或者在 LinkedIn、社交媒体上得到反馈时，我们也都会把它发到 Slack 里。我们当然也有合作伙伴关系，所以针对不同来源有不同频道，但那就是我说的意思。我需要 Claude 的帮忙才能跟上，因为进来（的反馈）实在太多了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay. So this is cool. So this is a way of working that you've built to stay on top of all the stuff shipping, which is this kind of daily ritual/routine where you as a manager look at what people are saying about the current state of Claude Code and Cowork and used to just like, "Okay, someone go fix this, go fix that." Now it's like, "Here's the PR that'll fix this thing. Check it out. We're ready to ship it if you want." Awesome.
turns.zh: 明白了。好。所以这很酷。这是一种你建立起来的工作方式，用来跟上所有在发的东西——就是这种每日仪式/例程：你作为经理，去看大家在说 Claude Code 和 Cowork 当前状态的什么，过去就是「行，谁去修这个、去修那个」。现在变成了「这是会修那个东西的 PR。你看看。你想发我们就准备好了」。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Obviously a big challenge for people is also just code review. I imagine Claude is also doing a lot of its own code review. Is there anything there you've recently figured out that allows your teams to ship faster stuff that they are confident is great?
turns.zh: 好。显然对大家来说另一个大挑战是代码审查。我猜 Claude 也在自己做很多代码审查。在那一块，你最近有没有琢磨出什么，能让你的团队更快地把东西发出来、而且他们有信心那东西很棒？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yeah. And honestly, it's crazy when you think we didn't even have Claude Code reviews last year. And so speak of bottlenecks, that was a really, really big bottleneck of the human reviewers. So we definitely, for the important areas that need deep subject matter expertise, we definitely want to make sure we have the proper humans still reviewing. I would say what helps us though is the more that we can automate to almost check in the framework for what good looks like. Claude is very good when you give it a framework to validate against those frameworks. (00:15:25): So I had mentioned recently we just updated the content design to have a skill in it. And this is why I think if you have specs or check those into the repo and then make sure the spec also keeps up to date with the code frequently. But that's what I found works really well of anytime you have a statement of what good looks like, get the end to the repo and then Claude Code review can make sure it's still matching what you set up to do.
turns.zh: 对。老实说，想想去年我们连 Claude Code review 都还没有，就挺疯狂的。说到瓶颈，那真的是人类 reviewer 的一个超大瓶颈。所以在那些需要深度专业知识的重点区域，我们绝对要确保仍有合适的人在审。但我想真正帮到我们的是：我们能越多自动化地植入「什么是好」的框架去检查。当你给 Claude 一个框架去对照验证时，它非常强。(00:15:25)：所以我刚提到，我们最近刚更新了内容设计，在里面加了一个 skill。而这也是为什么我觉得：如果你有 spec（规格说明），就把它们也 check in 进 repo，并确保 spec 也跟代码频繁保持同步。只要你有「什么是好」的明确表述、把它放进 repo，那么 Claude Code review 就能确保它仍然跟你设定要做的事对得上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And basically it's like the evolution of test driven development.
turns.zh: 而那基本上就是测试驱动开发（TDD）的进化版。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yes. For TDD, because I remember that was a big thing, my gosh, maybe like in the 2000s of the test first and then you can make sure the test fails, then you do actually the code. In principle is really good. But I know I remembered, I myself struggling a bit because it was almost like you have to eat the broccoli first because I was like, "Oh, you have to write this test first." And I just get so much thrill out of shipping and building product. So it's funny, actually the first bug I fixed on Claude Code, I remember asking Claude, "Hey, I want to do test-driven development. Help me write the test first, make sure it's fails and then we'll actually do the fix and then now the test passed." (00:16:32): And the fact that used to be that test generation used to just be this tax that I remember having to pay, the fact that that's now automated and you can even revisit all these principles that have been around for a while. But now they actually might be even more efficient just because you have the models that can do more of the work for you.
turns.zh: 对。说到 TDD，我记得那是件大事——天呐，大概 2000 年代那会儿——先写测试，然后确保测试失败，再写真正的代码。原则上真的好。但我记得我自己有点挣扎，因为那简直像「你得先吃西兰花」，我在想：「哦，你得先写这个测试。」而我一旦把东西发出去、把产品构建出来就会特别兴奋。所以有趣的是，我在 Claude Code 上修的第一个 bug，我记得问 Claude：「嘿，我想做测试驱动开发。帮我先写测试，确保它失败，然后我们再做修复，现在测试就过了。」(00:16:32)：而过去「生成测试」就像是我记得不得不交的一笔税，现在它自动化了——你甚至能重新捡起所有这些存在已久的原则。只是现在它们可能更高效，因为你有能帮你做更多工作的模型。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's so unfair. It just writes the test for you first. So on this point of builders, one of my favorite slides from your talk that I want to ask about is who you are hiring and what you look for in people. And so I'll read what you said there and I want to hear more here. So the two profiles that you now look for when you're hiring are creative builders with product sense and deep systems experts for the hard parts.
turns.zh: 对，那太不公平了。它直接先帮你把测试写了。顺着 builder 这个点，你演讲里我最喜欢的一页，我想问的是：你在招谁、你看重人的什么。我来读一下你那页说的，然后想在这儿多听你讲。你现在招人看的两个画像，是「有产品感觉的创造性 builder」和「负责硬骨头部分的深层系统专家」。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yeah. The deep subject matter expertise, for example, when I first joined Claude Code, we had really great product generalists and then I realized, oh, we were missing folks with systems background. And so that was definitely an area that we needed more folks with systems and distribute systems expertise. And so I would say it's all about trust but verify. The models are really good, but there are definitely a lot of areas that still need the verification. And so wherever you need the deep subject matter expertise, I would say that's an area to definitely still invest in. (00:17:54): And the other one is kind of like the product [inaudible 00:17:57], almost like the dreamers. These are folks that usually will be like, "My gosh, you're really passionate about a product." And they have an idea, they build it, and then it's always like looking at the feedback and then iterating and polishing and making sure that the product is a delightful experience. Owning that product end to end, that's another skillset that served us really well on Claude Code.
turns.zh: 对。深层专业知识，比如我刚加入 Claude Code 时，我们有非常棒的产品通才，然后我意识到：哦，我们缺的是有系统背景的人。所以那绝对是我们当时需要更多系统、分布式系统专家的领域。所以我想这归根结底是「trust but verify（信任但要验证）」。模型确实很强，但绝对有很多领域仍然需要验证。所以只要你需要深层专业知识，我想那绝对是仍然值得投资的一块。(00:17:54)：另一个差不多是「产品 [听不清 00:17:57]」那种，几乎是梦想家。这类人通常像：「我的天，你真的对某个产品充满热情。」他们有个想法，就把它做出来，然后总是去看反馈、去迭代、去打磨，确保这个产品是个令人愉悦的体验。端到端地拥有那个产品，是另一种在 Claude Code 上对我们极其好用的技能组合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This super resonates. There's this word ambition. I don't know if you used it, but that's what I thought of as you were talking. That's been coming up a bunch recently in the podcast and other work I've been doing. There's this 10xC engineer I was talking to the other day and he was just like, "I heard about a feature idea." Someone's like, "Hey, we should build this. " And I was like, "No, that's really hard and complicated." And he's like, "But now I'm like, no, no, that's so possible. I just ask Claude Code to do it and he just does it."
turns.zh: 这特别有共鸣。有个词叫「ambition（雄心）」。不知道你有没有用，但你说的时候我想到的就是它。这最近在播客和我做的其他工作里频繁出现。前几天我聊到一个 10 倍工程师，他就说：「我听到一个功能想法。」有人讲：「嘿，我们应该做这个。」而我本来会说：「不，那真的又难又复杂。」而他说：「但现在我会想，不不，那太 possible 了。我直接让 Claude Code 去做，它就做了。」

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's this whole mindset shift and he's just realizing now it's about how ambitious can you be. Everything is now possible in theory. Now it's about how ambitious and how big can you think versus just like, okay, it's all these stupid little features and things they have to unblock. Does that resonate? Is that something that you think about?
turns.zh: 这是一种整体的心态转变，他刚意识到：现在的问题是你敢有多大的雄心。理论上一切皆有可能。现在的问题是你能想多大、多 ambitious，而不是「行，就是这些愚蠢的小功能、还有那些得去 unblock 的事」。这有共鸣吗？是你也会思考的东西吗？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yes. Actually, I was just catching up with an engineer yesterday and he actually is not a mobile engineer by trade, but we really needed to update this feature to also have a mobile footprint. And it was just amazing. He's like, "You know what?" And it's common because you might think, wait, but I'm not like an Android expert. But now, thanks to Claude, actually I can actually have a partner and actually also do this on the mobile surfaces. And so that definitely resonates. It's lifted the ceiling of what anyone is able to do.
turns.zh: 有。其实我昨天刚跟一个工程师聊，他本职其实不是移动端工程师，但我们真的需要把这个功能也扩展到移动端。而太神奇了——他说：「你知道吗？」这很常见，因为你可能会想「等等，但我又不是 Android 专家」。但现在，多亏了 Claude，我真的可以有这么一个搭档，而且还能在移动端表面上做这个。所以这绝对有共鸣。它顶高了任何人能做到的上限。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let me follow that thread, as the role has transformed in such a crazy way, some people are thriving, some people super frustrated, unhappy, fighting, resisting. What do you see common across the people that are doing really well, the engineers that have adapted and are thriving versus the engineers and even outside engineering that are just frustrated and having a bad time?
turns.zh: 那顺着这条线——既然这个角色以这么疯狂的方式变了，有些人如鱼得水、有些人超级沮丧、不开心、在对抗、在抗拒——你在那些做得特别好的人（适应了、如鱼得水的工程师）和那些（甚至工程之外的）只是沮丧、过得糟糕的人之间，看到什么共同点？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: I would say a growth mindset really, really helps. Actually, even before AI tooling, I found that has been just so valuable. And I learned that a lot. Actually, it was the shift from Microsoft to Meta. That first year I'm like, "Oh, this is what having a growth mindset really means." It's really this concept of always be learning, also what served you to get you to this point may not serve you no longer. But it's really hard because of course everybody, we've all gotten to the state by acting or operating in a certain way. And so sometimes it is a little bit scary to think, "Wait, but I've been successful so far. You're asking me to change what has made me successful." (00:20:48): And so I would say the growth mindset has really served me well and I think it's also served others well that I noticed like always leaning in with curiosity and always being able to learn. And then in terms of the frustration, I think sometimes I also see a little bit of fear. And so my advice there is, at least this is how just in life, because we all have... And fear is of course an evolutionary, I didn't study anthropology, but I think it makes sense, right? It helps us make sure we were able to survive and not get eaten by larger predators. (00:21:27): But for anything that there is a fear, my advice is kind of lean in and ask, "Okay, what can I do about it? What is within my control?" Because sometimes the frustration comes from fear and feeling like everything is outside of my control and so it's happening to me. And so if you think about, "Okay, what is in your control instead of happening to you, is it happening for you? And then what's something that you might be able to do and change?" I felt that's been helpful, because if not, it is super frustrating to have the fear and then feeling like everything's outside of your control. (00:22:04): I actually remembered when I was in, actually when I was in high, it's funny when we were going back to IBM, when I was in high school, I actually didn't go into computer science or engineering. I really wanted to be a visual artist and this is how far back we go. Back then, computers were really expensive. So I actually didn't even have access to a computer. My first access to computer was grade nine, I think in high school. I don't even know if this happens in high school anymore. My high school had a typing class where you went to class just to learn how to type on a keyboard and learn to be really proficient and that was my first time and then the next class was maybe like some HTML programming. (00:22:45): So anyways, but the reason why I fell in love with it was what I love about art is creating and being able, if you have an idea, you can go ahead and create and tell a story. And then I realized, oh, computers and programming, that enables me to do that. So anyways, I tried to really fast try to make up for all the science classes for me to get into university, but I had this fear of, "Oh, but how will I afford to get into an engineering school?" And it was this big unknown. I grew up in Ontario, so I was very grateful. I knew there was an Ontario School Assistance Program, OSAP, I think, which I'm very grateful for. But I didn't know how much of that would cover my tuition or expenses and it was just this unknown and it would be like a year out. (00:23:29): And I remember thinking, "Okay, what can I do about it?" And then as luck would have it, the National Bank of Canada just posted this flyer in our high school saying, "Hey, we're hiring high school interns to be a bank teller." And I remember, and of course it was going to be minimum wage, but I thought that could be a lifeline. But it was funny because the class I hated the most in high school was accounting, so I don't know if it would be any good at it at all. But I signed up to be a bank teller and that ended up being such a great decision because I worked all summer, saved up. (00:24:00): And then actually I was able to work as a bank teller on the weekends. So I would go to school Monday through Friday and then on Saturdays be a bank teller. And that ended up being this lifeline that enabled me to pay for all my school expenses. And we talked about the year 2000 dot com crash that when folks weren't hiring as much interns actually, I continued being a bank teller for two years. But that was the one action I felt I could take that was within my control to try to counter this fear I have of, "If I'm really going to go down this path, I don't even know if I could have afford to go to school." (00:24:38): So that's probably my other advice of growth mindset and the source of frustration or anxiety. If it's coming from the like, see, is there one action that's within your control that you can take. There was a saying do some things. What would you do if you're not afraid actually? Those were my two favorite things before like, "What would you do if you're not afraid and do something scary once in a while?" Because-
turns.zh: 我会说成长型思维（growth mindset）真的、真的很有帮助。其实早在 AI 工具出现之前，我就发现它已经极有价值。而且我学了很多。其实是从微软转到 Meta 那次。头一年我就在想：「哦，这才是真正拥有成长型思维的意思。」就是这种永远在学、而且「曾经让你到达这个点的东西，可能不再服务于你了」的概念。但这真的很难，因为当然每个人都是靠某种方式行动/运作才到达现在这个状态的。所以有时会有一点吓人：「等等，但我到目前为止都成功了。你让我改变那个让我成功的东西？」(00:20:48)：所以我想成长型思维对我很好用，而且我想它对其他人也很好用——我注意到那些人总是带着好奇心迎上去、总是能学。而说到沮丧，我想我有时也会看到一点点恐惧。所以在那个点上我的建议是——至少这是我在生活中应对的方式，因为我们都有……而恐惧当然是进化来的，我没学过人类学，但我想这讲得通，对吧？它帮我们确保能活下来、不被更大的捕食者吃掉。(00:21:27)：但对任何让人恐惧的事，我的建议是去迎上去、问：「好，我能为此做点什么？什么是我能控制的？」因为有时沮丧来自恐惧、来自「一切都超出我的控制、是发生在我身上的」这种感觉。所以如果你去想：「好，什么是你能控制的，而不是发生在你身上的——它是为你而发生的吗？那有什么是你或许能做、能改变的？」我觉得那很有帮助，因为如果不这样，带着恐惧、又觉得一切都超出控制，会超级沮丧。 (00:22:04)：我其实记得，当我……其实当我在高中时——有意思，我们刚回溯到 IBM，我在高中时其实没去学计算机或工程。我真的想当个视觉艺术家，我们这渊源有多深就多深。那时候电脑超贵。所以我其实连电脑都碰不到。我第一次接触电脑是九年级，我想是在高中。我甚至不知道现在高中还有没有这个。我高中开了个打字课，你专门去上课就为了学怎么在键盘上打字、练到特别熟练——那是我第一次接触，然后下一门课大概是某种 HTML 编程。(00:22:45)：总之，我之所以爱上的原因是：艺术让我爱的，是「创造」——而且只要你有个想法，你就能去创造、去讲一个故事。然后我意识到：哦，电脑和编程，能让我做这个。所以总之，我拼命想把我落下的科学课补回来，好进大学，但我有个恐惧：「哦，但我怎么付得起去上工程学院？」那是个巨大的未知。我在安大略长大，所以我特别感恩。我知道有个安大略助学计划，应该是 OSAP，我特别感激。但我不知道它能覆盖多少学费或开销，而且那是一年之后的事，完全是未知。(00:23:29)：我记得我在想：「好，我能为此做点什么？」然后运气好，加拿大国家银行刚好在我们高中贴了张传单说：「嘿，我们在招高中生当银行柜员实习生。」我记得，那当然是最低工资，但我想那可能是根救命稻草。 (00:24:00)：但有趣的是，我高中最讨厌的课是会计，所以我都不知道我到底能不能干好。但我还是报了名去当银行柜员，而那最后成了个极好的决定，因为我整个夏天都在工作、攒钱。而且实际上我周末也能当银行柜员。所以我周一到周五上学，周六当柜员。那最后成了根救命稻草，让我能支付我所有的上学开销。我们也聊过 2000 年那次互联网崩盘——当大家不那么招实习生时，我其实又当了两年银行柜员。但那是我觉得在自己掌控范围内、能采取的一个行动，用来对抗我那个恐惧：「如果我真要走这条路，我甚至不知道我付不付得起上学。」(00:24:38)：所以那大概是我关于成长型思维、以及沮丧或焦虑来源的另一条建议。如果它来自恐惧，看看：有没有一个在你掌控范围内、你能采取的行动。有句话叫「做点事」。「如果你不害怕，你会做什么？」那是我以前最喜欢的两句话之一——「如果你不害怕，你会做什么」，以及「时不时做一件吓人的事」。因为——

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: ... Are my two favorite things before, like what would you do if you're not afraid and do something scary once in a while? Because that's also usually how we grow. I found that when you're really good and professional at what you do, you're kind of at peak maximum efficiency. But then how do you keep growing is you then do something scary that you might not have done before and yeah, you will have a dip because you need to learn, but that's kind of how you keep pushing yourself to learn.
turns.zh: ……是我以前最喜欢的两句话之一——「如果你不害怕，你会做什么」以及「时不时做一件吓人的事」。因为那通常也是我们成长的方式。我发现，当你在自己做的事上变得真正厉害、专业，你其实处在最高效的状态。但你怎么继续成长？就是你去做一件你以前可能没做过的吓人的事——对，你会有一个低谷，因为你需要学，但那基本上就是你不停 push 自己去学的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The quote that I have probably used the most on this podcast of all quotes is, "The cave you fear contains the treasure you seek."
turns.zh: 我在整个播客里用得最多的引语大概就是：「你恐惧的洞穴，藏着你寻找的宝藏。」

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Oh, I love that.
turns.zh: 哦，我爱那句。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And it's so true. I forget who put this, but just the thing that is scariest is like, that's a compass towards that's what you should be doing. In terms of career.
turns.zh: 对。而且它太对了。我忘了这话谁说的，但意思就是：最吓人的东西，像个指南针，指向你该去做的事。在职业上。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: I'm going to steal your quote.
turns.zh: 我要偷你的这句话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, please do. Don't do all the scary things. Maybe don't jump off a cliff, but maybe in career moves, it's probably a good choice. So kind of following this path, something that I know that is important to you, something you think about that I also think about is this kind of gap that is forming between people that are just leaning into AI, killing it, doing super well, and then people that are just not. And this is a scary time for people that may be left behind in this new world that is emerging. I know you spent a lot of time with small businesses; that's a big passion of yours, to help people learn how to use AI in their work. Talk about just how you think about that and what maybe we should be thinking about to help folks stay, not fall behind basically.
turns.zh: 对，请便。别去做所有吓人的事。也许别跳崖，但在职业选择上，那大概是个好选择。顺着这条路——我知道对你很重要、你也思考过、我也思考过的一件事，就是这种正在形成的鸿沟：一边是全力拥抱 AI、杀疯了、做得极好的人，另一边就是没有的人。对这个正在浮现的新世界，这可能是一个让人害怕的时期，怕被落下。我知道你花了很多时间跟小企业在起；那是你的一大热情——帮人们学怎么在工作里用 AI。聊聊你是怎么想的，以及我们大概该思考什么，来帮大家——基本上就是不落后。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Oh, I love this. Yeah, it's one of my passion topics because I kind of mentioned growing up in Canada and I moved there when I was a kid. I was born in Hong Kong so I didn't speak any English and my parents had to work all the time. So my grandma who is the best grandmother anyone could have ever asked for. I know everybody thinks their grandma's the best, but I really was so lucky I had the best grandma. She moved with us just to take care of me while my parents were working, but neither of us spoke English, but I was able to learn how to speak English by going to school and speaking with classmates. And when I think about my grandma, it was very alienating for her to be in a new country where, and back then it wasn't as walkable. (00:27:12): But one summer I remembered we just happened to find this little yarn shop that was owned by a lady that also spoke Cantonese. And so that became every week we would go to this yarn shop the summer. My grandma found her knitting circle and then I think I learned how to do macrame, which I think is having a comeback by the way. It's always funny to see what's-
turns.zh: 哦，我爱这个。对，这是我的热情话题之一，因为我刚提到在加拿大长大，我是小时候搬过去的。我出生在香港，所以一句英文都不会说，而我父母得一直工作。所以我奶奶——那是任何人能奢求的最好的奶奶。我知道每个人都觉得自己的奶奶最好，但我真的太幸运了，有个最好的奶奶。她跟我们一起搬来照顾我，因为我父母在上班，但我们俩都不会说英文，而我通过去学校、跟同学说话学会了说英文。而想到我奶奶，对她来说身处一个陌生国度是很疏离的——那时候也没现在这么好走。(00:27:12)：但有个夏天，我记得我们碰巧找到了一家小毛线店，店主也是个说粤语的女士。所以那个夏天我们每周都去那家毛线店。我奶奶找到了她的编织圈，然后我想我学会了做 macramé（马克拉梅编织），顺便说那门手艺我在看来要回潮了。看什么在回潮总是挺好笑的——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Macrame coming back.
turns.zh: Macramé 要回潮了。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Macrame. I think, yeah. Heard it here first on Lenny's podcast. I think macrame's coming back.
turns.zh: Macramé。我想，对。在 Lenny 播客这里先听为快。我想 macramé 要回潮了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好了。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: But that was probably where my love came from. I'm like, oh wow, this little small business created this wonderful sense of community. And I've been really fortunate to become friends with all of the small businesses that I love. So that's kind of like where the passion comes from. And then how it happened was I was using Cowork for my own business expensing travel. I don't know what it is. I really don't like doing business expensing. And when I was using Cowork, it was magic. I'm like, "All these things that I don't like to do, like Cowork is doing for me." And I'm like, "Wait a minute, all my friends," and honestly, small business owners, they really bust their butt. They work incredibly hard and sometimes might be operating on really small margins. (00:28:20): And so I thought if Claude Cowork is so good at helping me do my little business travel expense, this would be huge for it. Because I see my friends sometimes sitting at the bar with stacks of bills and all they're doing is invoicing and expensing and I think nobody actually really likes to do it. So that's kind of where it came from. And then so yeah, I remembered helping a couple of them onboard and it was also very humbling to see them go through our onboarding flow. Actually, they found some really good bugs. So it was really like a win-win, but it was also delightful for me because they also use Cowork in ways that I wouldn't have thought about because I was all fixated on, look at how it is amazing with PDFs and invoice. (00:29:02): And then one of my friends who runs two restaurants, she's like, "Oh my gosh, this folder I have is like a junk drawer of, like it's basically our documents folder. It just becomes this junk drawer of every, or downloads, just like the kitchen junk drawer." And she's like, "I know I have a few menus in here and I can't find it." And I'm like, "Well, let's ask Cowork." So we gave Cowork access to directory, found the menus. And then she use in a really unique way. She goes, "I want to make sure I keep my prices reasonable for locals and tourists." So she goes, "Hey, Claude, look across my style of cuisine in this area. Is it comparable?" And it came back with really cool, almost like market analysis. And she goes, "Hey, I actually just went to that restaurant in Seattle and that was pretty good." So I learned something every time. And yeah, they've been giving me great feedback as well.
turns.zh: 但那大概就是我热爱的来源。我在想，哦哇，这家小本生意创造了这种美妙的社区感。而且我跟所有我喜欢的小企业都成了朋友，真的很幸运。所以热情就是从那儿来的。而它怎么发生的呢——我当时在用自己的 Cowork 来报销差旅。我不知道怎么了，我真的超不喜欢做商务报销。而当我用 Cowork 时，那就是魔法。我在想：「所有我不喜欢做的事，Cowork 都替我做了。」然后我在想：「等等，我所有朋友」——老实说，小企业主，他们是真拼命。他们工作极度努力，有时可能利润薄得要命。(00:28:20)：所以我想，如果 Claude Cowork 在帮我做我的小本差旅报销上这么好，那对他们会是巨大的。因为我看到我朋友有时坐在吧台前，面前一堆账单，他们所做的无非就是开票、报销，而我想没人真的喜欢做那个。所以那就是它的由来。然后我记得帮其中几个 onboard，看他们走我们的 onboarding 流程也让我很谦卑。其实他们还找到了一些很好的 bug。所以简直是双赢，而且对我也很愉悦，因为他们用 Cowork 的方式是我根本想不到的——因为我满脑子都是「看它在 PDF 和发票上多厉害」。(00:29:02)：然后我一个开了两家餐厅的朋友说：「哦我的天，我这个文件夹就像个废物抽屉，基本就是我们的文档文件夹。」 它就成了这个每个……或者 downloads 里的废物抽屉，就像厨房的废物抽屉。她说：「我知道我这里面有几份菜单，但我找不到。」我说：「好，咱们问 Cowork。」于是我们给了 Cowork 访问那个目录的权限，找到了菜单。然后她用了个特别独特的方式。她说：「我想确保我对本地人和游客都保持合理定价。」所以她说：「嘿 Claude，看看我这片的菜系风格。有可比性吗？」它回来了一份特别酷的、几乎像市场分析的东西。她说：「嘿，我其实刚去了西雅图那家餐厅，还挺不错的。」所以每次我都学到东西。而且对的，他们也一直给我很棒的反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the question then is just like, how do we spread this to everybody? Because a lot of people are just like, "I don't have time for this" or "I hate AI." It's just like, I want to ignore it. Is it like talking, is it just talking about these, sharing examples? What do you think? What's a way to make a dent in this problem?
turns.zh: 所以问题就是：我们怎么把这个扩散给所有人？因为很多人就是：「我没时间弄这个」或者「我讨厌 AI」。就那种，我想忽略它。是靠聊、靠分享这些例子吗？你怎么看？怎么才能在这个问题上啃出个洞？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: For all of us, especially to your listeners, are probably very AI-pilled. If there's anyone either in their community or their family that has like... I would start with what has something that you really have felt has made a meaningful life change for you with the AI tools and then seeing if that is a conversation starter for... Because for me, AI is a tool. Again, it's the whole light in the dark. I totally understand the frustrating part as well. But for me, I'm also felt like knowledge is power. Have to learn how to use the tools because it could actually be the light part of that light and dark equation. So I think that's something that I would love everybody's help with, whether it's a community member or even if there's a business you really like and you think, "Hey, have you ever..." It's a little awkward to start. (00:30:56): I remember when I first reached out to my friends, I'm like, because I don't talk about what I do with them a lot, but I'm like, "Hey, I kind of work in AI. Can I..." It's even unnatural for me to do it because I'm like, "Hey, can I show you what Cowork is possible?" But we ended up having a lot of fun. So yeah, I would love for, like that conversation starter would be great of, yeah, because I just want to make sure we keep sharing the knowledge and making the tool equitable because if not, I'm concerned that the divide grows larger and larger.
turns.zh: 对我们所有人，尤其对你的听众，你们大概都已经被 AI 武装得很彻底了。如果你们社区里或家里有人……我会从「有什么你真的觉得用 AI 工具给你生活带来了有意义改变的东西」开始，然后看那能不能成为一个对话的开头……因为对我而言，AI 是个工具。再次强调，它就是黑暗中的那束光。我也完全理解那让人沮丧的部分。但对我而言，我也觉得知识就是力量。得学会怎么用这些工具，因为它可能正是那个「光明与黑暗等式」里光明的一侧。所以我想这事我特别需要大家的帮助，不管是社区成员，还是哪怕有家你真的很喜欢的企业、你觉得「嘿，你有没有……」开头会有点尴尬。(00:30:56)：我记得我第一次联系我朋友时，我在想，因为我不太跟他们聊我做什么，但我在想：「嘿，我大概在做 AI。我能……」对我而言连做这个都不自然，因为我在想：「嘿，我能给你看看 Cowork 能做什么吗？」但我们最后玩得特别开心。所以对的，我会希望——那个对话开头会特别好，因为我想确保我们持续分享知识、让工具更平等，因为如果不这样，我担心这道鸿沟会越拉越大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Me too. I find that sharing use cases, as you said, is so powerful. I was just using Cowork the other day to fill out my son's camp forms and just sharing that on Twitter, just like a lot of people are like, "Oh wow, I didn't think about that." Yeah. It's just like these little things you don't think about that Cowork and Claude Code can do. (00:31:47): Kind of along those lines, speaking of Cowork, if you think about it, Anthropic has been super early on uncovering these really big opportunities ahead of everyone else. For example, coding. So far ahead, like realizing this is a huge market. Whether it was intentional or not, it was just like, whoa, that's maybe the biggest new business opportunity in history. And then Cowork is a great example, just leaning into knowledge work. Let's just solve all knowledge work. Why not? So far ahead of everyone else. Another element is it feels like a focus on the personality of the model, something you all were very early on, just how important that is, not just for the experience, but just also the intelligence and success of the model. What is it that you think Anthropic and the teams do differently that allows you to uncover these opportunities and then just go big on them before other labs, let's say?
turns.zh: 我也是。我发现就像你说的，分享用例特别有力量。我前阵子刚用 Cowork 填我儿子的夏令营表格，就把它发在 Twitter 上，很多人就说：「哦哇，我没想到这个。」对。就是这些你不会想到 Cowork 和 Claude Code 能做的事。(00:31:47)：顺着这条线，说到 Cowork——如果你想想，Anthropic 一直超级早地发现了这些远远领先于所有人的巨大机会。比如编码。超前那么多，像意识到这是个巨大市场。不管是有意无意，就是「哇，那可能是史上最大的新商业机会」。而 Cowork 是个绝佳例子，就是全力拥抱知识工作。我们干脆把一切知识工作都解决掉。为什么不？远远领先于所有人。另一个元素是，它感觉像是聚焦于模型的「人格」——你们很早就在做，就是它有多重要，不只为了体验，也为了模型本身的智能和成功。你觉得 Anthropic 和这些团队做的什么不一样的事，让你们能在其他实验室之前发现这些机会、然后就大举投入？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Well, I haven't worked in any other labs, so I'm not sure how labs operate, but I will share like, yeah, with... And actually on the Claude Code team as well and Cowork, we also keep an eye on latent demand. Now, we're very fortunate with coding as a use case because so many ads that we were like our own first customers and we're able to do really rapid feedback. But latent demand has been like a, for example, like Cowork we noticing a lot of folks that were not necessarily coders were using Claude Code. Can we make that experience better? (00:33:15): I think that's actually even outside of Anthropic, that served me well in all the different products I've worked on. And actually it's funny you mentioned the Claude for my passion with small business. After I had a few of those visits, we ended up now launching Claude for Small Business, which is really cool because I, and it totally didn't come from me, so I'm not taking credit, but I noticed it too of like when I was working because they were asking me, "Oh, does it have this plugin or at this plugin?" I'm like, "I think it does." And then we have to go and search for it. (00:33:45): So actually now Claude for Small Business bundles it all up. So inside Cowork, you just have this little toggle and there was a wonderful team that's been doing Cowork sessions with small businesses that probably found, "Hey, we could have an efficiency gain here or make the experience better." And so I would say always, not only for products that you're on, like making sure you're always listening to feedback and always iterating, trying to make a delightful, reliable, high quality experience, but then also keeping an eye out for, "Oh, what are these other use cases that are popping up? And can we also make that experience better?" It's interesting. In software, I've learned that customers will use your product in ways that you did not intend for good or for bad. And so the best way is really, it's all about the iteration, learn and keep close to the feedback.
turns.zh: 嗯，我没在其他实验室工作过，所以不确定实验室怎么运作，但我会分享——对的，在 Claude Code 团队和 Cowork 上，我们也盯着潜在需求（latent demand）。现在我们在编码这个用例上很幸运，因为很多广告里我们自己就是第一批客户，能做极快的反馈。但潜在需求一直是像——比如 Cowork，我们注意到很多未必是 coder 的人在用 Claude Code。我们能把那个体验做得更好吗？(00:33:15)：我想那其实在 Anthropic 之外，也在我做过所有不同产品上对我很好用。而且有意思的是你提到了我对小企业的热情。在我做了几次那样的拜访后，我们最后上线了 Claude for Small Business（面向小企业的 Claude），那特别酷，因为我——而且完全不是来自我，所以我不居功，但我也注意到了——就像我当时在工作时，他们在问我：「哦，它有这个插件吗、或者有那个插件吗？」我说：「我想有。」然后我们还得去搜。(00:33:45)：所以现在 Claude for Small Business 干脆把它全打成一个包。在 Cowork 里面，你只要拨一下这个小开关，就有个超棒的团队一直在跟小企业做 Cowork session，他们大概发现了：「嘿，我们在这儿能提效，或者把体验做得更好。」所以我想总是——不只对你负责的产品，要确保你一直在听反馈、一直在迭代，努力做出令人愉悦、可靠、高质量的体验；同时也要注意：「哦，还有哪些其他用例在冒头？我们也能把那个体验做得更好吗？」这很有意思。 在软件里，我学到：客户会用你的产品，用在你没打算的方式上——无论好坏。所以最好的方式其实就是：一切关于迭代、学习、并贴近反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Weight and demand. That term's come up a bunch on this podcast. There's some there. Might be some there. So essentially, it's just watching closely for behavior that you may not have expected or that it's just kind of emerging and then just going big on that essentially, exploring it, building something awesome.
turns.zh: 潜在需求（latent demand）。这个词在本播客出现过好几次了。里面可能有点东西。可能有。所以本质上就是：密切观察那些你可能没预料到的、或者正在浮现的行为，然后就大举投入——去探索它，做出很棒的东西。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yeah. And having a hypothesis for, hey, because actually when you see people jumping through hoops to make something work, can you actually make that an even like, a smoother and better experience?
turns.zh: 对。而且带着一个假设——嘿，因为其实当你看到人们为了把某件事搞通而各种绕弯子时，你能不能把它做成更顺滑、更好的体验？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Coming back to the way that your teams operate, you guys are so at the edge of what's possible and the role of just engineering has changed so much. I'm curious what you think is the next kind of frontier of how engineering in particular is going to change. Is it like fleets of agents? Is it something else? Just what's the next big shift to how engineers operate that either you're already working on or implementing or just is starting to happen?
turns.zh: 对。回到你们团队的运作方式——你们处在可能性的最前沿，而工程这个角色已经变了这么多。我好奇你认为下一个前沿、尤其是工程会怎么变。是 agent 集群（fleets of agents）吗？还是别的什么？就是工程师运作方式的下一次大转变——要么是你已经在做或在落地的，要么是正开始发生的？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: I would say we're shifting more towards async, like asynchronous. And so to your point, the fleets of agent, like that's why routines is so interesting because it's almost like I used to be doing a prompt and synchronously and then I would maybe kick off different props asynchronously, but now I can actually have a routine that actually generates these prompts for me. So it's almost like the level of abstraction keeps pulling up a little bit. And so yeah, I wish I have a crystal ball to see what this is going to look like. It'd be fun actually for you and me to revisit a year from now.
turns.zh: 我会说我们正更多转向异步（asynchronous）。所以顺着你说的，agent 集群——就像这就是为什么 routines 这么有意思，因为以前我同步地写个 prompt，然后可能异步地 kick off 不同的 props，但现在我其实可以有个 routine 来替我生成这些 prompts。所以抽象层级一直在往上提一点。对的，我真希望我有个水晶球能看看这会是什么样。其实一年后你我来复盘会很有意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, I want to hear more about this. So help us understand what is routines and then when you say synchronous, you're writing a prompt and it just kind of goes off and is it writing it immediately? Talk about what this actually looks like.
turns.zh: 不，我想多听这个。帮我们理解 routines 是什么，然后你说「同步」时，你是在写个 prompt、它就跑掉了、是立刻写出来吗？讲讲这实际长什么样。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Ah. Yeah. So routines is like how you can... So if you remember, I was chatting about my... What I used to do is always wake up with my morning cup of coffee and, "Hey, look through this Slack channel for me." But then now I have a routine that I set to run every morning at a certain time.
turns.zh: 啊。对。所以 routines 就像你能……还记得我在聊我的……我以前的做法总是：端起早上的那杯咖啡，「嘿，帮我把这个 Slack 频道过一遍。」但现在我有个 routine，设成每天早上某个固定时间跑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like a chronic job.
turns.zh: 它就像是份长期挂着的活儿。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: To say hey. That's right. But then it's able to actually go and kick off agents on your behalf because even before it would be, oh, you could, yeah, do a chronic job to automate, but now it's, "Hey, look at these feedback." And then if you're seeing some of these bugs, that what are some polish fixes that you might be able to knock out? And then it would go kickoff and then I wake up and I end up having PRs that I could review versus before, which is still more of AI can have different agents. (00:37:05): And then I'm still thinking about, okay, now what do I do with this information? So it's like that higher level abstraction of, okay, now how can I actually write a routine that also basically does prompts for me for spawning different agents? So I think we'll move more towards that kind of asynchronous style of working.
turns.zh: 就像说嘿。没错。但现在它其实能代你去 kick off agent，因为哪怕是以前，哦，你可以，对，做个长期挂着的活儿来自动化，但现在它是：「嘿，看看这些反馈。」然后如果你看到一些 bug，那有哪些打磨性的修复是你能顺手敲掉的？然后它就 kick off，然后我醒来，最后就拿到我能审的 PR——而不是以前那种，虽然那也更多是有不同 agent 的 AI。(00:37:05)：而我还在想，好，现在我拿这些信息干嘛？所以就像那个更高层的抽象：好，现在我能怎么写一个 routine，让它基本也替我生成去 spawn 不同 agent 的 prompts？所以我想我们会更多往那种异步的工作风格走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So interesting. So in a sense as a manager, you have these kind of things you do daily and what you're saying here is you can set up these prompts that kind of check in every day on the things you would be doing. Like how are the projects going? What's falling behind? What should I unblock? Who's struggling? And how do I improve some polish? And so the idea here, what you're describing here is write these things that you almost do as a manager daily and have Claude essentially do them for you and then show you, here's what I'm doing, here's what there is to review.
turns.zh: 太有意思了。所以某种意义上作为经理，你有些每天在做的事，而你这里说的是：你能设好这些 prompts，每天去 check in 在你本来会做的事上。比如项目进展如何？什么落后了？我该 unblock 什么？谁在挣扎？我怎么改进一些打磨？所以你描述的想法是：把你作为经理几乎每天在做的事写下来，让 Claude 本质上替你做，然后展示给你：「这是我在做的，这是有东西要你审的。」

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: And then it's even like, then giving even more autonomy at some point of, you know what, go for it. For example, a verification-
turns.zh: 然后甚至在某一点上给它更多自主权——你知道的，去搞吧。比如，一个验证——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:38:01].

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Is really good.
turns.zh: 真的很好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Go for it.
turns.zh: 去搞吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see. So you give it a little bit of freedom to do more of this?
turns.zh: 我明白了。所以你给它一点自由，让它做更多这种事？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. That is so interesting. It reminds me, speaking on this idea of go for it, like I wasn't planning to talk about this, but I just watched Tyler Cowen had this awesome talk about just like what's happening. I don't know if you know Tyler Cowen, this really smart dude, economist, has a podcast. There's so much talk of the people that are doing best in this world. His term is initiative. They have initiative. Another term people use, agency. Is that something just like, people hear this a lot, just like the people that seem to be doing best are taking the most initiative, getting the most proactive, have the most agency. Does that kind of spark any thoughts to you, just what people may need to, I don't know, think about or improve on?
turns.zh: 好。那太有意思了。它让我想到——顺着「去搞吧」这个点——我没打算聊这个，但我刚看了 Tyler Cowen 一个超棒的演讲，聊正在发生的事。我不知道你认不认识 Tyler Cowen，一个超聪明的人，经济学家，有个播客。现在有很多关于「在这个世界里做得最好的人」的讨论。他的词是「initiative（主动性）」。他们有主动性。别人用的词是「agency（自主能动性）」。这是不是那种大家听得很多的东西——就是那些似乎做得最好的人，是主动性最强、最主动出击、最有 agency 的？这会不会在你脑子里点亮什么想法，关于人们也许需要思考或改进什么？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Actually, I love that word: agency. That's what we really hold important on the Claud Code and Cowork team. But it's interesting, I say along with high, because we really, it's about like, "Hey, here's a problem." And then it's really everybody on the team has ideas for how to address the problem. So it's really high agency. And then we say with high agency, it's also high accountability. So it's all about making sure folks have that freedom to cook, but then it's also like, okay, what's the accountability for it as well? And again, it goes back to what's a hypothesis of what you're trying to solve. So I think, yeah, the balance like are almost like two sides are the same kind of agency and then accountability I think has served our team really well.
turns.zh: 其实我超爱「agency」这个词：那是我们在 Claude Code 和 Cowork 团队真正看重的。但有趣的是，我把它和「高」连在一起说，因为我们真的是——「嘿，这有个问题。」然后团队里每个人都有怎么解决这个问题的想法。所以那是真正的 high agency。然后我们说，高 agency 也意味着高问责。所以关键就是确保大家有那种放手去搞的自由，但另一方面也要问：那对应的问责是什么？再说一次，这回到「你想解决的假设是什么」。所以我想，对，这种平衡——几乎像同一枚硬币的两面——agency 和问责——对我们团队真的很好用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such an important element of agency. Okay, cool. Everyone's off doing stuff, but okay, what have you busted it up? What have you done? So kind of along those lines, it feels like there's this vibe shift recently from token maxing, just go crazy, spend as much as possible, just see what's possible to like, wait, what are we actually getting out of this? How much is it costing? What's the ROI? Interestingly, Boris was actually head of eng productivity at Meta. That was his job, is measuring eng productivity. And then also just this tweet of lines per code, like code shift. There's this interesting discussion of just how do you actually measure productivity increase and ROI of AI tools in spend? You guys have the unfair advantage of getting free tokens working in Anthropic. With that in mind, what have you learned about just how to measure say ROI of engineers in today's world?
turns.zh: Agency 真是太重要的元素了。好，酷。大家都在各搞各的，但好，那你搞出什么了？你做了什么？顺着这条线——最近好像有种 vibe 上的转变，从「token maxing（疯狂堆 token）、不管不顾、能花多少花多少、就看什么可能」，转向「等等，我们到底从中得到了什么？花了多少？ROI 是什么？」有意思的是，Boris 其实在 Meta 当过工程生产力负责人。那是他的工作——衡量工程生产力。而且还有那条「代码行数」的 tweet，像代码转变。有个很有意思的讨论：你怎么真正衡量 AI 工具投入下的生产力提升和 ROI？你们有个不公平的优势——在 Anthropic 内部能免费用 token。带着这点，你学到了什么，关于怎么衡量今天这个世界上工程师的 ROI？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: This eng productivity is such a fascinating topic. Yeah, because I remember even Boris mentioned like, "We'll first start with lines of code." And then I remembered once then there was a debate of, "Well, lines of code, this engineer had this crazy lines of code, but they just took some library and then just was porting it." So they checked it in and then I was like, "Well, maybe it's significant lines of code." And then it's, "Well, but what if we're updating our frameworks and now we're generating less code, but the output's still the same?" So now I was like, "Okay, maybe it's time to land PR." But it's very interesting of it's always been whichever metric, like if you're really focused on the out... My advice here is one is output, like is the output really going towards the outcome? Because yeah, the token maxing, it's almost like the lines that we code that we used to have, but I'm really much more about a, what is it that we're trying to do? (00:41:26): All of this... There was another saying I really like, "Don't forsake motion for progress." Because if you're measuring tool user usage, then you're measuring the action, but is it really making whatever the end outcome of yours important? And so I really try to zoom out and focus on what is the problem we're trying to solve, what's a good way to measure that. And then that's what we focus mostly on versus the productivity measurement. I would say though, outside of metrics, especially on teams as you're having more people adopt AI tooling, I would say definitely go on a listening tour for the leaders listening to a podcast. Especially, I love to focus on the senior engineers as well, like hear from them on what's working, what's not, how can we actually make it better because they will also help you multiply and scale that up across a full engineering team. (00:42:21): And sometimes it's those conversations where you might spark an idea that comes up and also really good shared learning versus metric dashboards. It's very interesting. I've learned some good lessons from metrics. I'm all about, like it's really great when you have a metric that you can actually help climb on, but always keep in mind of is, kind of my whole growth mindset of, is it still serving you? Always keep in mind like, is that metric really still serving the outcome that you were aiming for? (00:42:50): A fun example I have of this is in the early Facebook Marketplace days, we were kind of launching by region and we really wanted to make sure we're building a delightful product before we expand. And I remember in the early days, one thing we would keep an eye on is number of sellers. And I remembered after launching to our first region, I'm like, "Oh, in this area the number of sellers is low, but actually people are finding items that they're looking for," which is what we're aiming for or like helping people find items that they need. (00:43:19): And then I realized in that region it wasn't a large number of sellers, but there were power sellers. But our first gate before we expand would've just been factoring heavily number of sellers. And I remember that quick conversation of, hey, and this goes back to that whole people will use things in ways you may not expect and shift, iterate, learn. And so then we updated the metric to go, oh, it's not a number of seller because it didn't factor in power sellers. And so that's the advice I have too. Whatever metric, whether for productivity or even for product, always keep an eye and make sure that you're not just having blinders on that's blindly following a metric that used to make sense because sometimes the landscape can change so fast, even the metrics themselves might need to be adjusted.
turns.zh: 工程生产力真是个迷人的话题。对，因为我记得连 Boris 都提到：「我们先从代码行数开始。」然后我记得后来有个争论：「嗯，代码行数，这个工程师代码行数疯了，但他只是拿了某个库然后 port 了一下。」所以他把它 check in 了，然后我在想：「嗯，也许是「有效代码行数」。」然后又说：「可是，如果我们更新了框架、现在生成的代码更少了，但产出还是一样呢？」所以那时我就在想：「好，也许是「PR 落地时间」。」但很有意思的是，不管哪个指标，如果你真的聚焦在产出……我这里的建议之一是「output（产出）」——这个产出真的在奔着 outcome（结果）去吗？因为对，token maxing 几乎就像我们过去有的那种代码行数，但我更在乎的是：我们到底想做什么？(00:41:26)：所有这些……还有另一句我超爱的话：「别用运动（motion）替代进展（progress）。」因为如果你衡量的是工具使用率，那你衡量的是动作，但它真的让你真正重要的那个最终 outcome 发生了吗？所以我真的试着 zoom out，聚焦在我们想解决的问题是什么、有什么好方法去衡量它。然后那才是我们主要聚焦的，而不是生产力衡量。不过我想说，在指标之外，尤其当你有更多团队采用 AI 工具时，我绝对建议领导们去做一次「listening tour（倾听之旅）」——就像在听一个播客。尤其我爱聚焦在资深工程师上，听听他们什么 work、什么不 work、我们到底怎么把它变得更好，因为他们也会帮你把这件事在整个工程团队里成倍放大、规模化。 (00:42:21)：而有时就是那些对话，会点燃一个冒出来的想法，而且是真正好的共享学习——而不是指标看板。这很有意思。我从指标上学到了一些好教训。我完全支持——当你有个真的能帮你往上爬的指标时，那特别好；但永远记着：带着我整个成长型思维去想，它还在服务你吗？永远记着：那个指标真的还在服务你原本瞄准的 outcome 吗？(00:42:50)：我有个好玩的例子：在 Facebook Marketplace 早期，我们大概是按地区上线的，我们真的想在扩张前先确保做出一个令人愉悦的产品。我记得早期我们盯的一件事是「卖家数量」。我记得上线第一个地区后，我在想：「哦，这地区卖家数量低，但其实人们在找到他们想找的东西」——那正是我们瞄准的，或者帮人们找到他们需要的物品。(00:43:19)：然后我意识到，那个地区卖家数量不大，但有「power seller（大卖家）」。而我们扩张前的第一道门槛，本来会重重地只看卖家数量。我记得那次快速对话——嘿，这又回到「人们会用你意想不到的方式用你的东西」，然后转变、迭代、学习。于是我们更新了指标——哦，不是卖家数量，因为它没把 power seller 算进去。所以那也是我的建议。无论什么指标，无论是为了生产力还是为了产品，永远盯紧，确保你不是只戴着 blinders（眼罩）、盲目跟着一个曾经合理、但有时环境变得太快、连指标本身都可能需要调整的指标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this comes back to your process that you shared of having Claude watch all the PRs shipping per engineer, let's say, and then not focusing on the metrics, but focusing on that leading to a conversation about what impact does this have, what was maybe some bugs that happened and that being a really powerful way of understanding what's going on with this engineer. Awesome.
turns.zh: 这又回到你分享的那个流程：让 Claude 盯着每个工程师发的 PR，然后不聚焦指标，而是聚焦在「这引发一场关于它有什么影响的对话——发生了什么 bug」——而那成了理解这个工程师在干嘛的、极强的一种方式。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me come back to this, just this question of speed and quality and just impact. Is there anything else you've learned about just how to balance those things, just like this crazy velocity of code that's being generated and just staying on top of quality and impact. Is there anything else there that might be helpful to other teams that are trying to wrangle all these PRs being shipped every day?
turns.zh: 让我回到这个——速度、质量和影响力的问题。关于怎么平衡这些东西，你还有学到什么？面对这种被生成出来的疯狂代码速度，还要跟上质量和影响力。对哪些还在试图 wr角度每天发出来的这么多 PR 的其他团队，还有什么可能有帮助？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: I would say, and this is what honestly we want to keep doing more of and being better at it too. The proactive quality, so especially for quality, making sure that what are the experiences that are key and making sure you actually is, actually speaking of metrics, those are really good things that make sure you can see trends over time. And so on the quality front we found, and this is like the more proactive we can be of making sure we can get an earlier detection into quality. And so that's been one thing that we've been paying a lot of attention to. So I started this, "Hey, let's have a concept of what's bad versus what's sad." And bad is like a very bad irrecoverable error and sad is something that's kind of like a pain point, recoverable, but it's interesting when you stack up sads, it could generally go to bad. (00:45:39): But even starting with a high level framework like that and because if not, I think sometimes with dashboards you can have time to load or all these other, but when you're dealing with a lot of different product surfaces, it's harder to go, "Wait, is that a good number or not a good number?" And so one thing that's helped us is versus just raw performance or reliability numbers, also having some framework of what we think is a bad experience and making sure we're focused on addressing those and then also keeping an eye on where we're seeing in terms of the sad.
turns.zh: 我会说，而这其实也是我们想持续多做、并做得更好的。主动式质量（proactive quality），所以尤其对质量，确保哪些是关键体验、并确保你真的——说到指标，那些是能让你看到随时间趋势的极好东西。所以在质量这条线上我们发现，而且我们越主动、就能越早侦测到质量问题。那是我们一直很关注的一件事。所以我开了个头：「嘿，咱们有个概念——什么是 bad、什么是 sad。」bad 是一种极糟的、不可恢复的错误；sad 是一种有点像痛点、可恢复的——但有趣的是，当你把 sad 堆起来，它通常会演变成 bad。(00:45:39)：但哪怕从这样一个高层的框架开始也好，因为如果不这样，我想有时看板会有加载时间之类的问题，但当你面对很多不同的产品界面时，你会更难说「等等，那个数字好还是不好？」所以帮到我们的一件事是：除了原始性能或可靠性数字，还要有一个「我们认为什么是 bad 体验」的框架，确保我们聚焦在解决那些上，同时盯紧我们在 sad 上看到的情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: That helped us a little bit.
turns.zh: 那帮了我们一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I like the bad and sad. So these are like thresholds of this is bad. Okay, this is serious. And this is in terms of performance or failures or what sort of things are you measuring here?
turns.zh: 对，我喜欢 bad 和 sad。所以这些是像阈值——这是 bad，好，这是严重的。而这是就性能、或失败、或你在这里衡量的是哪类东西说的？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: So for example, we allow each team, like speaking of agency, so knowing that bad is like a really bad irrecoverable error, we enable each team of further surface areas or it could be services that they lead. So for example, on CLI could be crash rates, like a crash is pretty bad, you lost work. And for example, sad might be, "Hey, is it flickering?" It might be recoverable. But we have each team, and that's why it's been interesting because surface areas are different, we would have all these dashboards, but it's harder to zoom out and go, "Okay, what's the overall theme of the experience?" So to your point, we give high agency to each team of what we think constitutes a bad and what's a sad, and then what's the goal that each team wants to take.
turns.zh: 比如，我们让每个团队——说到 agency——既然知道 bad 是那种极糟的、不可恢复的错误，我们就让每个团队能进一步去定义他们的界面领域、或者他们负责的 service。比如 CLI 上可能是崩溃率，崩溃就挺糟的，你丢了工作。而 sad 可能是：「嘿，它在闪吗？」那是可恢复的。但我们让每个团队——这就是为什么有趣，因为界面领域各不相同——我们会有所有这些看板，但很难 zoom out 说「好，体验的整体主题是什么？」所以顺着你的点，我们给每个团队 high agency，让他们定义什么是 bad、什么是 sad，以及每个团队想达成的目标是什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The main takeaway I'm hearing here is one of the best tools for staying on top of quality is just monitoring and tests versus spending more time reviewing, which makes sense because the speed is just impossible to stay on top of. And it almost speaks to this idea of closing the loop for agents to be able to figure things out themselves. They know what success looks like, cool, we'll fix it ourselves. So that's a really interesting takeaway, is just invest more in the tests. Evals I imagine is part of this and then just monitoring failures and speed and things like that.
turns.zh: 我在这里听到的主要 takeaway 之一是：跟上质量最好的工具之一，就是监控和测试，而不是花更多时间审——这讲得通，因为那个速度根本不可能靠人跟上。而这几乎指向一个想法：为 agent 们「闭环」，让他们能自己搞清楚。他们知道成功长什么样，酷，那我们自己来修。所以那是个很有意思的 takeaway：就是多在测试上投资。我猜 evals（评估）是其中一部分，然后就是监控失败、速度之类的。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something, I think this is public. I know that you guys have this dashboard that tracks just like F-words, how often people are like, because they're so and frustrated. There's like a funny term for it, I think. I forget what it's called.
turns.zh: 有件事，我想这是公开的。我知道你们有个看板，专门追踪 F 开头的词（f-word）——人们有多经常说，因为他们太……沮丧了。有个挺好玩的叫法，我想。我忘了叫什么。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yes. Actually, I remember. Yeah, that was last September because we were all seeing some frustrations and yeah, that was an engineer on the team of, "Hey, we should maybe track swear words." I'm like, "Oh, that's a great idea." I remember it. I had just joined when we were having that really fun conversation. Yeah. So it's again, like it's very interesting to look at... And that's why evals is hard too because it's going back to that user experience and how we can make sure it's a delightful experience and less frustrating. But yeah, the swear word dashboard is a fun one.
turns.zh: 对。其实我记得。对，那是去年九月，因为我们都看到一些沮丧，对，那是团队里一个工程师说的：「嘿，我们也许该追踪一下脏话。」我当时说：「哦，好主意。」我记得。我刚加入时正赶上那次特别好玩的对话。对。所以它又回到——看这个很有意思……而那也是为什么 evals 也难，因为它回到那个用户体验、我们怎么确保它是个令人愉悦、更少挫败的体验。但对的，脏话看板是个好玩的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Mercury, radically different banking, loved by over 300,000 entrepreneurs and now with Command. I've been a customer of Mercury's for over six years. I have never once thought about leaving. Mercury is basically what happens when banking is built by product people, not by bankers. They make it so easy. Dare I say fun, to send invoices, move money around, set up virtual cards for folks on my team. Does your bank have an API, a terminal native CLI, or an AI-ready MCP server? I don't think so. And just recently they launched Command, a conversational interface built directly into Mercury, which acts as your financial operator. I've been using Command to transfer money around, to figure out what categories I've been spending the most money in, analyze my cash flows. And just today, I used it to find out how much I've made from a specific sponsor over the past year. (00:49:15): I just ask, how much have I made from X over the past year? 10 seconds later, I have an answer. It is so freaking cool. Visit mercury.com to learn more and apply online in minutes. Mercury is a FinTech company, not an FDIC insured bank, banking services provided through Choice Financial Group and Column N.A., members FDIC. (00:49:35): Kind of going back to the way you operate and ways that you've figured out to work in this crazy new world that we're in. I've heard about a couple things that you've implemented that are pretty unique, I think, to how teams operate and I think is something that has worked really well for you. One is making every manager start as NIC and then just every manager has to continue being NIC part-time, kind of this player, coach approach. Talk about that, why that's so important in today's world.
turns.zh: 本期节目由 Mercury 呈现—— radically different banking（彻底不同的银行），被超 30 万创业者所爱，现在还有了 Command。我是 Mercury 的客户已经超过六年了。我从未有一次想过离开。Mercury 基本上就是：当银行是由做产品的人、而不是银行家造出来的，会发生什么。他们把它做得那么简单。恕我直言，有趣——开发票、挪钱、给我团队的人设虚拟卡。你们的银行有 API 吗？有原生的终端 CLI 吗？还是有 AI-ready 的 MCP server？我想没有。而就在最近他们上线了 Command——一个直接内建进 Mercury 的对话式界面，充当你的财务操作员。我一直在用 Command 转钱、搞清楚我花钱最多的类目是什么、分析我的现金流。就在今天，我用它查出了过去一年我从某个赞助商那赚了多少。(00:49:15)：我就问：过去一年我从 X 赚了多少？10 秒后我就有了答案。它太他妈酷了。去 mercury.com 了解更多、几分钟内在线申请。Mercury 是一家 FinTech 公司，不是 FDIC 保险的银行，银行服务由 Choice Financial Group 和 Column N.A.（FDIC 成员）提供。(00:49:35)：回到你的运作方式，以及你在这个疯狂新世界里摸索出的办法。我听说过你落地了几件相当独特、我认为对团队运作很有用的事。一件是让每个经理都从 IC（独立贡献者）做起，然后每个经理都得继续兼职当 IC——这种 player-coach（球员兼教练）的方式。聊聊这个，为什么在今天的世界上它这么重要。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: I love it. It's funny, when I first join...
turns.zh: 我超爱。有趣的是，我刚加入时……

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: I love it. It's funny when I first joined, and I have amazing recruiting partners and I noticed this whole theme of growth mindset, it's just because the landscape is changing so fast. What worked well before may not make sense and even what makes sense today may need to change tomorrow. That's what I have to keep reminding myself. So yeah, when I first joined recruiters like, okay, yeah, we have these couple of manager postings and because actually how it came from a listening tour I did with all the members on the team, and I heard a lot of these, "Hey, I really appreciate the agency, but how can I make sure prioritization?" And so through that, and then there was some really good feedback too of making sure that it's not too many layers of reviews. There was good feedback. Some folks might have joined from other companies. (00:50:51): And I actually think as a leader, if you actually start as IC first without the worry of supporting people, because that's a very heavy responsibility, but before you have to take on that full responsibility, give yourself that maker time to actually dive deep into the code and learn the code base or the product, whatever it is. Honestly, the PRs I do, but it's more about for me, it's important because it keeps me in the flow because we're making so many changes to Cowork and code. So even me doing PRs, it's less about what it is I'm fixing. It's more about me using the product every day just to keep that touch, because as amazing as metrics and everything are, and I do look at those dashboards, as a leader, if you're not living and breathing your product every day, you sometimes lose the touch and feel of the product. (00:51:48): But anyways, on the manager front, I think giving time for managers that join to be able to go deep into do that before supporting people, and then they actually end up building really great rapport with the team, because if not, I think sometimes as managers, you might come and join a new team and you instantly think, "I have to manage. Let me dig into my manager toolbox and do manager-y things." But if you actually give yourself time to not have to worry about that first and actually learn what it's like to be an engineer and teammate on the team, that also goes really far to building rapport. In terms of using the product, I think that's important. It's interesting, every team I've joined, one of the first actually across all the different products, it could be VR, it could be smart glasses, it was like Instagram. (00:52:34): Usually when I first joined, one comment that comes back to me is, "Hey, you know what? I really love how you're actually using what we build." It's refreshing to see you giving user feedback, and so I think as leaders too, it's also a way for us to experience the work personally that the team does.
turns.zh: 我超爱。有趣的是，我刚加入时，我有超棒的招聘伙伴，而我注意到「成长型思维」这个主题贯穿始终，只因为环境变得太快。以前 work 的，现在可能不讲得通；而今天讲得通的，明天可能也要变。那是我得不断提醒自己的。所以对，我刚加入时，招聘伙伴说，好，我们有这几个经理职位——而它其实来自我跟团队所有人做的一次 listening tour，我听到很多：「嘿，我真的很感谢这种 agency，但我怎么确保优先级？」于是通过那个，再加上一些很好的反馈——确保评审层不要太多。有些反馈很好。有些人可能是从别的公司来的。(00:50:51)：而我觉得作为领导，如果你真的先以 IC 身份起步、不用操心支持别人的事——因为那是个极重的责任——但在你不得不扛下那全部责任之前，给自己那段 maker time，真正钻进代码、学代码库或产品，无论是什么。老实说，我做的那些 PR，但对我而言更重要的是：它让我保持在 flow 里，因为我们对 Cowork 和 Code 改得太频繁了。所以哪怕我做 PR，重点不在于我修了什么，更多在于我每天在用这个产品、保持那种触感——因为看板和一切再好，我也会看那些，但作为领导，如果你不是每天在呼吸你的产品，你有时会丢掉对产品的那种触感和感觉。 (00:51:48)：但总之，在经理这条线上，我想给新加入的经理时间去深入做那个、再去支持别人，然后他们其实会跟团队建立极好的默契，因为如果不这样，我想有时作为经理，你可能进来加入一个新团队，立刻就想着「我得管理。让我掏出我的经理工具箱、做经理该做的事」。但如果你真的给自己时间、先不用操心那个、而是去学「作为这个团队里的工程师和队友是什么感觉」，那对建立默契也走得极远。在「用产品」这件事上，我想那很重要。有趣的是，我加入的每个团队，跨所有不同产品——可能是 VR、可能是智能眼镜、可能是 Instagram——我刚加入时常听到一句反馈是：「嘿，你知道吗？我真的爱你在真的用我们造的东西。」看到你给用户体验反馈很 refreshing。所以我想作为领导，那也是我们亲自去体验团队所做工作的一种方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that people may not realize you were overseeing an organization of like 500 people at Meta before you moved to Anthropic and you moved to IC engineer basically and Anthropic from that.
turns.zh: 有件事大家可能没意识到：你搬到 Anthropic 之前，在 Meta 主管着大概 500 人的组织，而你基本上是以 IC 工程师的身份搬过来的——从那个到 Anthropic 的 IC。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: I started out, it was for a very short amount of time, but actually this was my journey between Microsoft and Meta. So at Meta, I interviewed as a manager, but I think at least for the first quarter, I was also an IC because I really wanted to learn what it's like to be a Meta engineer, because before then I was at Microsoft, cut my teeth on engineering at Microsoft. So I knew all the code bases, the tools, the languages, but it was so valuable to have those first months actually learn what it's like to ship as a Meta engineer. Plus it was also fun. I think sometimes we forget, but that's by the way, what I love about Claude Code because the last time I shipped production software at Meta was probably 2017, and every year, I do a lot of dogfooding and I also use dogfooding to help me vet the quality of product as well. (00:53:58): But it's been a very long time since I shipped production software, it's because part of it is I don't want to screw something up. I'm always so scared of what if I do something and then I cause a bug and then am I verifying everything properly, or am I wasting someone's time? Because also the tool flows would change, but I remember that first week on Claude, at first I almost again did my usual, let me go meet all the engineers and treat them to coffee, and then I'm like, "Oh wait, let me ask Claude." And so Claude was this really good onboarding buddy of mine because I was curious about the copays asking questions, and then it also really helped me do the automated test, but I also want to still do some manual testing, and I asked Claude, "Hey, help me come up with what's the way for me to manually test this to make sure I cover all the case." But all that then gives me confidence that okay, I can ship here again. (00:54:50): And then I got kind of more comfortable with it again, and so I've actually had a lot of friends reach out to me that have been managed for a while that's like, "Hey, I'm shipping code again, thanks to Claude." But in general, it's just important to me as leaders to make sure you're using the product that your team builds.
turns.zh: 我起步时，其实只做了很短一段时间，但那其实是我介于微软和 Meta 之间的旅程。在 Meta，我是按经理身份面试的，但我想至少在第一个季度，我也是个 IC，因为我真的想学「做 Meta 工程师是什么感觉」——在那之前我在微软，在微软把工程这一套练出来了。所以所有的代码库、工具、语言我都知道，但那头几个月去学「作为 Meta 工程师怎么发货」真的极有价值。而且它也很好玩。我想有时我们忘了，但顺便说，那也是我爱 Claude Code 的原因——因为我上次在 Meta 发生产级软件大概是 2017 年，而每年我都做很多 dogfooding，我也用 dogfooding 来帮我 vet 产品质量。(00:53:58)：但我已经很久没发生产级软件了，部分原因是我怕搞砸什么。我总那么怕：「要是我做了什么、然后搞出个 bug、那我验证得对吗？还是我在浪费别人的时间？」因为工具流也会变，但我记得在 Claude 的第一周，一开始我几乎又做了我惯常的事——让我去见所有工程师、请他们喝咖啡，然后我就在想：「哦等等，让我问 Claude。」所以 Claude 是我超棒的 onboarding 伙伴，因为我对 co-pay 好奇、问问题，然后它也真的帮我做自动化测试——但我也想还做一些手动测试，我问 Claude：「嘿，帮我想想，我手动测这个的方式是什么，确保我覆盖所有 case。」而所有这些给了我信心：好，我又能发货了。 (00:54:50)：然后我对它又更自在了些，所以其实有好多朋友联系我，他们管人管了一阵子，说：「嘿，多亏了 Claude，我又在发货代码了。」但总体上，作为领导，确保你在用你团队造的产品，对我来说就是重要的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so interesting that you are overseeing the team as an engine leader that is most changing the role of an engineer. It's such a meta role. The work of an engineer is transforming because of the software that you're building. One question along these lines is just do you worry about engineers' skills to code atrophying from not actually writing code anymore and does it even matter? Is this something you think about? Is it a big deal?
turns.zh: 有意思的是，你作为一个工程 leader 在主管这个最在改变工程师角色的团队。这角色太 meta 了。工程师的工作正因为你造的软件而在转变。顺着这条线有个问题：你会不会担心工程师「写代码」的技能因为不再真的写代码而退化？而这甚至重要吗？这是你会思考的事吗？是个大问题吗？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: It's interesting because we actually have this discussion on the team a bit. Are there things that we miss? Or actually to your point, I'm always thinking about when someone's onboarding and ramping, you have Boris who handrolled the code in the early days and of course now doesn't anymore, but he gained that knowledge from before because he was in the code base. So for especially all the engineers that join, I'm also like, make sure you're taking the time too to all the work that you do, still get the understanding of the architecture or the change because it goes back to that trust but verify. Maybe one day it won't matter anymore, but at the pace that we're going, I actually still think, it's always double clicking on that layer that you depend on. Maybe that to me is a meta. It's always take that time to learn about your dependencies because this way when your dependencies change, you're kind of more aware, or you might not be taking advantage of changes to dependencies. (00:56:31): So I think it's always about doing that double click, but the other thing that we found interesting on the Claude Code team is after a while we felt it could start being a lonely experience because we all started just working with our agents so much. So recently we started maybe a pairwise programming lunch because what we also learned was on Claude Code, everybody uses Claude Code Cowork. Everybody uses a flow so differently, and so we found that wow, when we do pairwise programming, we actually learn so much from each other, and then the other thing too is we make sure that we also have the maker time together too. So for example, hackathons is another thing we really like to do just to make sure we're kind of interacting together as a team.
turns.zh: 这有意思，因为我们团队里其实有点讨论这个。有没有我们漏掉的东西？或者顺着你的点，我总在想：当有人在 onboarding、在 ramp up 时——你有 Boris，早期亲手写代码，现在当然不写了，但他从以前获得了那种知识，因为他待在代码库里。所以尤其对所有新加入的工程师，我也说：确保你花时间在你做的所有工作里，仍然去理解那个架构或变更——因为这回到「信任但要验证」。也许有一天它不再重要，但以我们现在的速度，我其实仍然认为，要一直去 double click 你依赖的那一层。也许对我而言那是个 meta。总是花那个时间去学你的依赖，因为这样当你的依赖变了，你会更敏锐；或者你可能没有利用到依赖的变更。(00:56:31)：所以我想永远要做那个 double click，但我们在 Claude Code 团队发现的另一件有趣的事是：过了一阵子，我们觉得它开始变成一种孤独的体验，因为我们大家都越来越多地只跟自己的 agent 一起工作。所以最近我们开始了一个「pairwise programming lunch（结对编程午餐）」，因为我们学到的另一件事是：在 Claude Code 上，每个人用 Claude Code/Cowork 的方式都那么不同，所以我们发现——哇，当我们做结对编程时，我们真的从彼此身上学到好多；而另一件是，我们也确保有 maker time 是大家一起的。比如黑客松也是我们超爱做的，就是确保我们作为一个团队真的在一起互动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such a good point, just like the loneliness that emerges because used to be engineer teams building code together. Someone's doing backend, someone's doing front end, someone's doing iOS app, probably a bunch of people on the backend and it's like, " Well, if 10 Claudes running in parallel doing all these things," that is such a good idea of just finding ways to connect engineers. So the idea here is almost parallel programming but not. It's like parallel play when kids are grown up. You're kind of working next to each other but building your own things, but even just watching how other people build, your finding is really valuable.
turns.zh: 那是个太好的点了，就像那种浮现出来的孤独感——因为以前是工程师团队一起写代码。有人做后端、有人做前端、有人做 iOS app，后端大概还有一堆人——而「如果有 10 个 Claude 并行跑着做所有这些事」，那个「找到方式连接工程师」的点子太好了。所以这里的想法几乎是「parallel programming（并行编程）」但又不是。它像小孩长大后的 parallel play（平行游戏）。你们是挨着彼此工作、但建各自的东西，但哪怕只是看别人怎么 build，你的发现也真的很有价值。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
