turns.en: Yeah, and it's because our own tool chain is changing so fast as well, but yeah, it's very interesting to me. Everybody on our team just uses Claude Code and Cowork in different ways, and so every time I watch someone work, then I learn something myself as well.
turns.zh: 对，而且是因为我们自己的工具链也变得太快了，但对的，对我来说很有意思。我们团队每个人用 Claude Code 和 Cowork 的方式都不一样，所以每次我看别人工作，我自己也学到点什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you manage people getting over obsessed with their optimizing their workflows? Is there anything you're just like, "Okay, it's fine, just keep going."
turns.zh: 你怎么管理人过度痴迷于优化他们的工作流？有没有什么事你就是「好，没事，继续搞」？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: I haven't seen too many folks on our team. I think as everybody is just really excited about either an architecture update that we think will be higher reliability or some product experience. So most folks, that's what we talk about a lot. It's fun lunchtime conversations, but I don't think we over optimize because there's no perfect answer actually.
turns.zh: 我们团队我还没看到太多这种人。我想因为大家就是对某个架构更新（我们认为会更可靠）或某个产品体验超级兴奋。所以大多数人我们聊最多的就是这个。那是好玩的午餐对话，但我想我们不会过度优化，因为其实没有完美答案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's too much to do. These are really interesting insights. Just like as the role transformed, things come, things go. So I'm curious what else has kind of lost in this new world of software engineering. I used to be an engineer. I don't know if you know this. I was an engineer for 10 years, and it was like so fun just to sit there inflow coding, this feeling just like, "Oh wow, it's working. Look at it compiled. It's amazing. I'm making progress." And now you don't do that anymore. You just sit there and kind of wait for agents to build the thing. What else is kind of lost in this new world for engineers?
turns.zh: 有太多事要做了。这些真的是很有意思的洞察。就像角色转变时，东西来、东西走。所以我好奇，在这个软件工程的新世界里，还有什么「丢掉了」。我以前是工程师。不知道你知不知道。我做了 10 年工程师，那种就坐在那儿、在 flow 里写代码的感觉太好玩了——「哦哇，它 work 了。看它编译了。太神奇了。我在进步。」而现在你不再那么做了。你只是坐在那儿、等 agent 把东西 build 出来。对这个新世界里的工程师，还有什么「丢掉了」？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: It's so funny. I just had that conversation with the engineer and the team of talking about flow. Remember the old days you have this really gnarly problem and you pop that music soundtrack in, and then you're just in the zone? So yeah, and then there was always that big aha moment at the end I would remember. You remember being like, "You finally cracked it. Yay." So we do, but I think now we get a lot of joy from the product, but I do think because I hear from other engineers as well of well, some of the hardest parts is what I used to enjoy. Yeah, I heard that from another engineer as well, and so I think we're all just kind of shifting, but I do see the thing and that's why I was talking about the pairwise programming and the hackathon, that did recently come up more. Folks were starting to feel like it started to be a lonely experience.
turns.zh: 太好玩了。我刚跟那个工程师和团队聊过 flow 这个话题。记得以前你有这个超难的问题，你塞进那张音乐原声，然后你就进入 zone 了？对。然后我记得最后总有个大大的 aha 时刻。你记得那种「你终于破解了。耶。」所以我们在做，但我想现在我们更多的 joy 来自产品，但我确实觉得——因为我从其他工程师那也听到——「嗯，有些最难的部分是我以前最享受的」。对，我从另一个工程师那也听到这个，所以我想我们都在某种程度转变，但我确实看到那件事——也就是为什么我聊结对编程和黑客松，那最近更冒头了。大家开始觉得它变成了一种孤独的体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So interesting. Within Anthropic, I'm curious, so engineering the most transformed I think of any role right now, what's the second most transformed role so far would you say within Anthropic that's most different from how was like a couple years ago, let's say?
turns.zh: 太有意思了。在 Anthropic 内部，我好奇——工程我想是现在所有角色里变得最彻底的，那第二彻底的角色，你会说是哪个？跟一两年前比起来最不一样的？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: It's all the coding adjacent roles are shifting. I know you were chatting with Kat, I think PM is also transformed quite a bit because PM are no longer bottlenecked if they have an idea waiting on engineering bandwidth. So that's kind of like the next role that I saw on shift. Actually, our PMs have also helped us roll up sleeves and help shift some features when there was something we wanted to do, and an engineer wasn't able to. So I think it's all the coding adjacent roles are starting to shift, but I think that's where again, the verification is important because when you have more different disciplines checking in, how do we make sure everybody has higher confidence? I also think we need to do more to keep automating these other portions of the workflows. For sure, we focus a lot on coding, but next when you think about design or data science, those are starting to be the next areas that I think are good opportunities for us to see how we can start improving the experiences there as well.
turns.zh: 所有跟编码相邻的角色都在变。我知道你跟 Kat 聊过，我想 PM 也变了不少，因为 PM 如果有想法、不用再等工程带宽，他们就不再是瓶颈了。所以那大概是我看到的下一个在转变的角色。其实我们的 PM 也帮我们卷起袖子、在我们想做某个功能、而工程师又抽不出身时去帮忙推一下。所以我想所有跟编码相邻的角色都开始转变，但我想那也是验证重要的地方——因为当有更多不同学科的人在 check in，我们怎么确保每个人都有更高的信心？我也想我们需要做更多，去持续自动化工作流的其他部分。当然我们聚焦很多在编码上，但下一步当你想到设计或数据科学，那些开始成为我想到的、我们能看看怎么也开始改善那里体验的下一个领域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, speaking of data science, I have a data science friend and he was just saying how data science is so different now where now most of their job is people doing their own not amazing data science work using AI, and then just showing it to the data scientists, "Here, here's the analysis I did. Can you just make sure it's right?" And half the time it's not right, and so the job is just a whole different job now instead of doing the work that they thought they wanted to do. Now it's like, "All right, I'm just reviewing all this AI data science all the time. What the hell?" Along the lines, coming back to just how your team operates and how things are changing, let me see if something comes with this question. What should an engineering manager expect from their team now versus a couple of years ago, what's a normal, I don't know, baseline expectation of how things should work other than just we're shipping faster, is there anything else?
turns.zh: 对，说到数据科学，我有个数据科学朋友，他刚说现在数据科学多不一样——现在他们大部分工作是人用 AI 做着自己不咋地的数据科学活儿，然后就拿给数据科学家：「喏，这是我做的分析。你确认下对不对？」一半时间它都是错的，所以这个工作现在整个变成了另一种工作，而不是做他们本来想做的工作。现在是：「行吧，我整天就在审这些 AI 数据科学的东西。搞什么？」顺着这条线，回到你团队怎么运作、事情怎么在变，让我看看这个问题会引出什么。一个工程经理现在该从团队期待什么、跟一两年前比？什么是正常的、我不知道、baseline 的期待——除了「我们发得更快了」，还有别的吗？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Oh, interesting. Well, definitely I think most commits are Claude assisted, and so that was a shift. I think I kind of mentioned we have Slack channels with all the feedback and also our dashboards that we have gave to Claude. I think having engineers keep building that stronger product sense muscle is I think also another, and I think that in general helps with these really strong-minded product engineers. I would say more of these roles that were traditionally non-engineering, you do now see engineers, and sometimes you're just blocked by waiting for a cross-functional partner. I think there's less of those blocks now just because the models are able to augment additional capabilities that you may not have as an engineer.
turns.zh: 哦，有意思。对，绝对我想大多数 commit 是 Claude 辅助的，所以那是个转变。我想我刚提到我们有装着所有反馈的 Slack 频道，还有我们给 Claude 的那些看板。我想让工程师持续练强「产品感」这块肌肉，也是另一件事；而我想总体上那帮到有这些真正强产品心智的工程师。我会说，更多这些传统上非工程的角色，你现在确实看到工程师——有时你只是被等一个跨职能伙伴给卡住了。我想现在那种阻塞更少了，只因为模型能 augment 你作为工程师可能没有的额外能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it's kind of interesting. It's both directions. Engineers becoming more product-minded and responsible for the quality and success of a product, and then everybody becoming an engineer more and more.
turns.zh: 所以这挺有意思。它是双向的。工程师变得更有产品心智、对整个产品的质量和成功负责；而每个人变得越来越像工程师。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yeah, that's right. Yeah, it's all blurring.
turns.zh: 对，没错。对，一切都在模糊化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I forget who said this, but there's this like, " What is a role anymore?" And this guy said that it's like, "What's the average of what you do? What's the highest percentage of what you do, and that's kind of your role now," whatever it is to be.
turns.zh: 对，我忘了谁说的，但有句话大概「角色到底是什么？」这人说：「你做的事里，平均占比最高的是什么、占比最大的那部分，差不多就是你现在角色」——无论它是什么。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. I want to come back to your point about obsession with the product. Living, breathing, the product, dogfooding. I talked to a bunch of people that work with you about you, and that's the thing that came up most, just your obsession with living and breathing the product, using the product constantly, whatever it is you're building, this idea of dogfooding. Talk about just why that is so important, why that's something you instill within your teams and reports.
turns.zh: 哦天呐。我想回到你那个「痴迷于产品」的点。呼吸产品、dogfooding。我跟好几个和你共事的人聊过你，而那是最常冒出来的事——就是你对「呼吸产品」的痴迷，持续不停地用你造的产品，无论它是什么，这个 dogfooding 的想法。聊聊为什么它这么重要，为什么你会把它 instill（灌输）进你的团队和下属里。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Oh, love it. Yeah, I think it's really and this has worked for me. It's just been a really good way for me to keep a pulse. Anytime you build product, there's a dream. You're really hoping to enable an experience or making an experience better. So I think that helps me keep really close to the pulse. I also think, and maybe for sure on Visual Studio, that was where I got this love of it, but it's interesting because even Marketplace, I remembered once in a while, even after I left the team actually, one time I had a MacBook Air I wanted to sell. I'm like, "Oh, I haven't sold anything on Marketplace." And I could not believe it the minute I put it up for sale, a seller or buyer tried to scam me, and it was an interesting new scam vector I didn't detect, but that goes to, again, people will use your products in ways that you may not expect. (01:05:04): And so especially as leaders or even anyone on the team, we all have different life, actually, it's funny when I was supporting the VR and AR teams, somehow how I used VR, the setup, I would always be able to find these really weird floor height issues. So that ended up being a, "Oh, I'm going to help us," because somehow I got a good repro environment, and so I think it's number one, that's how you keep your pulse on the product that you're building and don't get too lost in metrics and dashboards only, or presentations.
turns.zh: 哦，爱了。对，我想它真的——而且这对我一直很好用。它对我而言一直是保持 pulse（脉搏）的极好方式。任何你做产品，都有个梦想。你真的希望能促成一种体验、或让一种体验更好。所以我想那帮我跟 pulse 贴得极近。我也想，也许在 Visual Studio 上肯定是这样——那是我获得这份爱的源头——但有趣的是，哪怕 Marketplace，我记得有次，其实在我离开团队后，有次我想卖一台 MacBook Air。我在想：「哦，我还没在 Marketplace 上卖过东西。」而我简直不敢信——我一把东西挂上去卖，就有个卖家或买家试图骗我，那是个我没察觉到的、有意思的新诈骗向量——但这又回到：人们会用你意想不到的方式用你的产品。(01:05:04)：所以尤其作为领导、甚至团队里任何人，我们都有不同的生活——其实好玩的是，我在支持 VR 和 AR 团队时，不知为何我用 VR 的方式、那个 setup，总是能找到这些超怪的地面高度问题。所以那最后成了「哦，我能帮上忙」，因为不知为何我有个好的复现环境。所以我想第一点就是：那是你保持对你所造产品 pulse 的方式，而且别只迷失在指标和看板、或者 PPT 里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's such an important point you're saying there that I just want to make sure people here is just like there's always this idea of anecdotal evidence and just examples versus the data, and what you're saying here is as a product leader, as an engineer leader, you've found a lot of success in the anecdotes, the specific little one-offs that you experience as a user versus obsessing with the data only.
turns.zh: 我想你刚说的那点太重要了，我只想确保大家听到：总有个「anecdotal evidence（轶事证据）和具体例子 vs 数据」的张力，而你这里说的是——作为产品领导、作为工程领导，你在那些轶事、你作为用户亲身经历的那些具体的一次性事件里，找到了很多成功，而不是只痴迷于数据。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yeah, and actually sometimes it's also how I've been able to most effectively help the team. So for example, the last team I was on, I was leading a VR team and because back then I have not checked in any code into that code base just because I was really worried about messing up the operating system, but what was a gap? We were doing a lot of polish fixes and I'm like, "Hey, you know what? I'll use my job fitting time to actually vet how the experience looks." And so that was also probably a way that I felt I could still meaningfully contribute to help hold the quality bar for the team, and then like I say, every team member usually always really appreciates because I think as a lead leader, you're supporting folks on team that outside of metrics and everything, everybody really wants to make sure their work matters and just making sure that leaders use your product. I think folks feel the leaders, and then remain really engaged and not too distanced.
turns.zh: 对，而其实有时那也是我能最有效地帮到团队的方式。比如我上一个团队，我带的是个 VR 团队，因为那时我根本没往那个代码库里 check in 过任何代码——就因为我超怕搞坏操作系统——但缺的是什么？我们在做很多打磨性修复，而我就在想：「嘿，你知道吗？我会用我的 dogfooding 时间，去实际 vet 那个体验长什么样。」所以那大概也是我觉得自己仍能有意义地贡献、帮团队把质量线撑住的一种方式；然后就像我说的，每个团队成员通常都超级感激，因为我想作为领导，你在支持团队的人——在指标和一切之外——每个人都真的想确保自己的工作有意义，而确保领导在用你的产品。我想大家会觉得领导「在场上」，然后保持真正投入、而不至于太疏远。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this connects a lot with your point that engineers need to become more product minded, that engineers need to become more PM-y, but this is like as an engineer, this is one way to do it. Use the product constantly and that'll help you understand what is missing in the product as a user because you're just using it.
turns.zh: 而这跟你说的「工程师需要变得更有产品心智、需要变得更 PM 化」很连通——但这是作为工程师、做这件事的一种方式。持续不停地用产品，那会帮你在作为用户时理解产品里缺什么，因为你就在用它。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: That's right, and I would say if you're leading a team where it's really hard for you to use a product, then meet with customers. Whatever that other avenue is, I think that's also been really important too. Every time I've done customer visits, I always learn something new. Actually, I remember that was Facebook Marketplace, we're trying to launch to Latin America and so we were testing in Chile, and I remembered it just wasn't doing as well as the other regions. Everything else, we've tried it and then I remember, I'm like, oh yeah, and we had a really small research trip where I went to Chile and I remember getting us a whole bunch of Android phones for us. It was very small crew, like just three of us, and upon landing and upon me opening up these Android phones and I'm like, ah, the LTE connection was much slower than what we were used to in the US. (01:08:09): So I'm like, "Oh, the Marketplace feed didn't even load very well on these low LTE situations." What a growth block that you can't even load, but again, that's why it's so important to always listen to customer feedback and get that fast feedback loop.
turns.zh: 没错，而我想说，如果你带的团队让你很难去用某个产品，那就去见客户。无论那条替代路径是什么，我想那也一直很重要。每次我做客户拜访，总能学到新东西。其实我记得那是 Facebook Marketplace，我们想上线拉美，所以在智利做测试，我记得它做得就是没其他地区好。其他都试过了，然后我记得，哦对，我们有次很小的调研之行，我去了智利，记得给我们弄了一堆 Android 手机。队伍很小，就我们三个，落地后我打开这些 Android 手机，我在想：啊，LTE 连接比我们在美国习惯的慢多了。(01:08:09)：所以我在想：「哦，Marketplace 的信息流在这么低的 LTE 情况下连加载都加载不好。」那是个连加载都加载不出来的增长 blocker——但再说一次，那就是为什么「永远听客户反馈、拿到那个快速反馈环」这么重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it was Jeff Bezos that said if you have data and you have an anecdote, trust anecdote over the data, surprisingly and that's a great example. Okay, just a couple more questions. One is in your talk, you had this really interesting slide at the end of what questions you're kind of thinking about right now that you haven't figured out how to solve with how much it's changing. I'm going to read the three. I'm curious just like if it's still these three, if there's anything else like current problems we need to figure out that we haven't solved in how we operate. What you shared in your talk was do we still need separate iOS and Android organizations? How far do you push fully on automated reviews, and with role blurring, how do you ensure everyone's equally productive? Still problems, is there anything else that you're thinking about like, "Okay, we need to crack this. We haven't figured this out."
turns.zh: 我想那是 Jeff Bezos 说的：如果你有数据、也有一个轶事，出乎意料地，信轶事胜过信数据——那是个绝佳例子。好，就剩几个问题了。一个是在你演讲里，结尾有张特别有意思的 slide，列着你现在在想、但还没想清楚怎么解的、随变化而变的问题。我来读这三个。我好奇它们还是不是这三个，有没有别的——我们需要想清楚的、还没解决的、关于我们怎么运作的当前问题。你在演讲里分享的是：我们还需要分开的 iOS 和 Android 组织吗？全自动审查你推到什么程度？而随着角色模糊，你怎么确保每个人都同样有生产力？还是这些问题吗，有没有别的你在想的——「好，我们得攻克这个。我们还没想清楚。」

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: You know the iOS Android one, I think and actually it's funny because speaking of the deep expertise, we definitely feel that it's really important to still bring on folks with those expertise, but we probably don't need as large because people are flexing. So it's again, making sure we have the Android and iOS experts, but then less of the larger kind of like mobile art one per, but again, that's still a balance that we're trying to figure out, do we have the right and enough expertise? Sorry, what was the second one?
turns.zh: 那个 iOS/Android 的，我想——其实有趣的是，说到深层专业知识，我们绝对觉得把有那些专业知识的人招进来仍然非常重要，但我们大概不需要那么庞大的规模了，因为人们在 flex（灵活跨界）。所以又是：确保我们有 Android 和 iOS 专家，但不再是以前那种「每个移动端各一大块」的规模——不过再说一次，那仍是我们想搞清楚的平衡：我们有没有对的、足够的专业知识？抱歉，第二个是什么来着？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh yeah, it is how far do you push fully, automated review?
turns.zh: 哦对，是「全自动审查你推到什么程度？」

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yes. Actually, well, this is a fun one with the content design check. I think we're looking for across all of it, how do you actually get what good looks like? And so actually the verification is still one that I think, and that's kind of like the second and the third that I think there's a lot more opportunities there for us, but the how far to push, I think looking at where we think experts still matters and then also again, have to keep asking ourselves, okay, is there a way to leverage that expertise to also automate? I think looking across the whole end-to-end experience, making sure we're not missing, I think we come at it from an engineering standpoint, but making sure on experiences how we think about those other areas. I think there's definitely still more that we can do there.
turns.zh: 对。其实，嗯，这个跟内容设计检查有关，挺好玩的。我想我们在整体上看的是：你怎么真正搞到「什么是好」的样子？而所以验证仍然是那个——我想那是第二和第三点里我们还有很多机会的，但「推到什么程度」，我想是看我们认为专家仍然重要的地方，然后再一次问自己：好，有没有办法 leverage 那个专业知识也去自动化？我想拉通整个端到端的体验来看，确保我们没漏掉——我想我们是从工程视角切入的，但要确保在体验上我们怎么思考那些其他领域。我想那绝对还有更多我们能做的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Basically, how do you set up a verification that the experience is what you wanted it to be?
turns.zh: 基本上就是：你怎么搭一个验证，确认那个体验是你要的样子？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Exactly, and I think that one is still a hard one to crack because you kind of mentioned evaluations because some of it for sure is accuracy, but it's also that experience. So that's something that we're still kind of thinking through.
turns.zh: 没错，而我想那一个仍然难啃，因为你刚提到 evals（评估）——因为其中一部分肯定是准确性，但也是那个体验。所以那是我们还在某种程度思考的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Is there anything else that's like, "Oh, this has changed recently. We got to figure out how to rethink the way we operate," or is this kind of the big ones?
turns.zh: 太棒了。有没有别的像「哦，这个最近变了。我们得想清楚怎么重思我们的运作方式」，或者这几个就是大的？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: I think because with routines and everything being more async, I think there is starting to be a high load on our context switching because I even remember myself, I was like oh, I kicked off, and so I think that's probably another thing we have to think about whether for team members or users, how can we actually make the experience better to reduce that load? Because I do see the context switching load increasing.
turns.zh: 我想因为 routines 和一切变得更异步，我觉得开始出现一种上下文切换的高负载了——因为我甚至记得我自己，我在想「哦，我 kick off 了」，所以我想那可能是我们得思考的另一件事——无论对团队成员还是用户，我们怎么真的把体验做得更好、去降低那个负载？因为我确实看到上下文切换的负载在增加。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you have 20 agents running, there's just endless checking in and reviewing and you have to remember what you were doing there. It's like such an interesting world where the idea flow we talked about before, like engineers and most people, there's less of the just hours of flow, but now the agents can kind of just remind you, "Here's where you're at." The reset to switch almost is easier because you don't have to relearn everything. You don't have to reunderstand the code base and the architecture. You can kind of just like, "Okay, but here's what we're trying to do." It's kind of like both, got better, got worse.
turns.zh: 如果你有 20 个 agent 在跑，那就有无穷无尽的 check in、审查，而你得记住你在那干嘛。这世界真有意思——我们之前聊的「flow（心流）」，像工程师和大多数人，那种连续几小时 flow 变少了，但现在 agent 能某种程度提醒你：「这是你目前的进度。」那种重置切换反而更容易了，因为你不用重新学一切。你不用重新理解代码库和架构。你可以某种程度就说：「好，但这是我们想要做的。」它有点像，既变好、又变坏。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Well, it's interesting because I used to book out focus time, the focus time for coding because you want that dedicated, and then the whole context switching, and then it's interesting now that because I can context switch more with more async agents, I'm noticing I do actually have to go back and block a focus time for me to catch up on all the different async work that I've kicked off.
turns.zh: 对，有意思的是，我以前会预约 focus time 来写代码，因为你要那段专注，然后还有整个上下文切换——而有趣的是现在，因为我能用更多异步 agent 来上下文切换，我注意到我其实得回头、给自己 block 一段 focus time，去赶上我 kick off 的所有那些不同异步工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, do you have any thoughts on the solution there? Because that's hard just like people just want to do more and more, and just how do you do that without constantly context switching? It's really hard and annoying.
turns.zh: 对，在那块你有什么解决思路吗？因为那很难——人们就是想做越来越多，而你怎么做才不一直上下文切换？真的又难又烦。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yes, I agree.
turns.zh: 对，我同意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Open question.
turns.zh: 开放问题。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Definitely I haven't cracked it yet.
turns.zh: 绝对我还没攻克它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So interesting. Okay, there's a question I thought of as we were talking that I'm so excited to hear your answer on that. I wasn't even planning to ask this, but it's so important these days, which is just like engineering jobs and hiring. So interesting that you would think AI would make engineers less necessary. On the other hand, it feels like you guys are hiring engineers like crazy, OpenAI's hiring engineers like crazy, just there's so much demand for engineers. Where do you think this goes? What do you think about just the future of the end role? And this big question, but just thoughts?
turns.zh: 太有意思了。好，有个问题，我们聊的时候我想到的，我超兴奋听你的答案。我本来甚至没打算问这个，但它现在太重要了——就是工程岗位和招聘。有意思的是，你会以为 AI 会让工程师变得没那么必要。但另一方面，感觉你们在疯狂招工程师，OpenAI 也在疯狂招工程师，对工程师的需求就是那么大。你觉得这会走向哪？你对这个终端角色的未来怎么想？这是个大问题，但就说说想法？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Actually, I'll share some vulnerability here. Speaking of big open questions, I really do think how we grow the next generation just because how you and me got to our engineering path is just so different. It's almost like okay, now when you graduate from school, it's like, "How do you fast-forward?" But the important thing to me, but still understand that double click I talked about to the layer of a need, but that is a big question I have, and I wish I have the answers, but I wonder if it's for software engineering, it's almost like you go more towards a fellowship or apprenticeship program. I know it's odd because technically we have internships that would, but those were kind of like three months and little projects, but I do wonder, and I wish I have a crystal ball here, but it's like how do you almost cram, and maybe it won't matter, but some of the life experiences that we all got, how do you actually enable us to teach that to the next generation of builders?
turns.zh: 其实在这里我分享一点 vulnerability（坦诚脆弱）。说到这种大开放问题，我真的在想我们怎么培养下一代——只因为你和我的工程之路走得那么不一样。几乎是：好，现在你从学校毕业，就像「你怎么快进？」但对我重要的，是仍然理解我说的那个「double click 到你需要那一层的依赖」，但那是我有的一个大问题，我希望我有答案，但我在想：对软件工程来说，它几乎像你更多走向一种 fellowship（研究员计划）或 apprenticeship（学徒制）项目。我知道这奇怪，因为技术上我们有实习，但那些更像是三个月、小项目，但我确实在想——我希望我有个水晶球——但就像你怎么几乎把我们都拥有的那些生活经验「 cram（塞）」进去，也许它不重要，但那些我们所有人获得的生活经验，你怎么真正让它们被教给下一代 builder？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right, if you don't have to ever look at code, what's the incentive for a new software engineer to truly understand how infrastructure works and memory allocation, all these things that are kind of foundational?
turns.zh: 对，如果你从不用看代码，一个新软件工程师去真正理解基础设施怎么运作、内存分配，所有这些基础性的东西，动力从哪来？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: And it's interesting, maybe the models will get good enough that it doesn't matter.
turns.zh: 而有趣的是，也许模型会好到那个程度，以至于它不再重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You don't have to worry about it.
turns.zh: 你不用操心那个。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: But I do think there's something about that double click because I think that's where there might be an opportunity to improve the product or the system, but figuring out how to learn that not necessarily by years of-
turns.zh: 但我确实觉得那个 double click 里有点东西，因为我想那可能是个改善产品或系统的机会——但要想清楚怎么学那个，未必要靠多年的——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Of typing code.
turns.zh: 靠敲代码。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Like years of-
turns.zh: 就像多年的——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Of typing code.
turns.zh: 靠敲代码。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Somebody's got to have to understand code at some level. It's like some Cobalt engineer they have to pull out of that retirement one day. Do you remember how to write Python?
turns.zh: 对。总得有人在某种层级上理解代码。就像某个 Cobalt 工程师，有天得把他从退休里拉出来。你还记得怎么写 Python 吗？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: You know actually what's really fun, one of my previous managers, he started software engineer when it was punch cards and it's so fabulous. He's been messaging me everything he's been building with Claude Code and I'm like, wow, what a career that you go from. He's really seeing this whole change. So maybe I think for us to think about is when I think about his career, how he got started with punch cards was also totally, totally different than now. I think it'll be interesting for us to see what remains important and then what changes in terms of importance and then it's like how do you gain... I have a theory, maybe that's what is important will shift over time. And then how do you build the proficiency in doing that?
turns.zh: 你知道其实特别好玩——我以前有个经理，他刚开始做软件工程师时还是打孔卡（punch cards）的时代，那太 fabuluous 了。他一直在给我发他用 Claude Code 构建的所有东西，我在想：哇，这是怎样的职业生涯啊，从那种起步到现在。所以也许我想的是：当我看他职业生涯，他从打孔卡起步，跟现在也完全是两码事。我想我们会很有意思地看到，什么依然重要、然后重要性上什么在变——然后就像你怎么获得……我有个理论，也许「重要的东西」会随时间转变。而那你又怎么建立做那件事的熟练度？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, just learn the things that really matter. The argument that I constantly hear is just like it's a new level of abstraction, just like assembly and binary. It just keeps going up and up. And now, okay, we don't need to actually look at the code. It's like a new layer of traction, prompts and Claude's thinking messages.
turns.zh: 对，就是去学那些真正重要的东西。我总听到的论点是：这就是新一层的抽象，就像汇编和二进制。它一直在往上提。而现在，好吧，我们不用真的去看代码了。那就像一层新的 traction（牵引层）——prompts 和 Claude 的 thinking 消息。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yeah. And it's maybe like, okay, what is an interesting problem and what's the prioritization for experience to build? It's interesting. Yeah. And then when you build things, how do you know it's actually resonating and it's doing what you intended?
turns.zh: 对。而它也许是：好，什么是个有意思的问题、而为了构建那个体验、优先级是什么？这很有意思。对。然后当你 build 东西时，你怎么知道它真的在 resonate（引起共鸣）、而且在做你原本想做的事？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's good. Yeah. Are we just building a bunch of slop here or is this actually this architecture that will work? I think the advantage though for young people is it's so much easier to just lean in and work in this new way versus being stuck in the way that things used to be. It's rare. It's amazing how many longtime engineers like yourself have adapted and embraced this. It's like so hard to just change everything. Okay, let's do it. Everything.
turns.zh: 而对，那很好。我们是在这儿造一堆 slop（垃圾）呢，还是这真的是个能 work 的架构？不过对年轻人来说优势在于：以这种新方式 lean in、去工作，比困在旧方式里容易太多了。这很罕见。这么多资深工程师——像你——都适应并拥抱了它，这太惊人了。要改变一切真的好难。好，做吧。全部。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Well, because the rate of change is also so fast. Actually, that was the one thing of, I remember the first time it was probably Sonnet 35 or 36 and I remembered it was still making some mistakes when I was doing things on the side. I'm like, "What are you doing?" And then what I noticed was some of the engineers that were resisting AI tooling, they're like, "Ah, but see, look at all of these." But then I think it was hard to understand of how the exponential rate of improvements. And maybe that's another interesting thing that I, myself, I'm learning too. There might've been something I tried to automate that Claude wasn't quite good enough. And then actually in the next model, oh, well, now it is good enough. So it's always also thinking about what may have not worked. It might be worth the time to revisit because that now might be a new capability.
turns.zh: 对，因为变化的速度也那么快。其实那是件事——我记得第一次大概是 Sonnet 3.5 或 3.6，我在做 side 项目时它还在犯些错。我在想：「你在干嘛？」然后我注意到的是：那些在抗拒 AI 工具的工程师，他们说「啊，但你看，所有这些……」但我觉得他们很难理解那种指数级的改善速率。而也许那是另一件我也在学的有意思的事。可能有些我试着自动化的事，Claude 当时还不够好。然后其实到了下一个模型，哦，嗯，现在它够好了。所以也要一直想：有什么之前不 work 的，也许值得再回去看看，因为它现在可能是个新能力了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. That comes up a lot on this podcast. Just build something that is almost working that is at the edge because once the model gets there, you'll be so far ahead of everybody else. Okay. Final question. You may have already answered this with what you just said, but what keeps you up at night?
turns.zh: 对。这在本播客出现很多次。就是去 build 一个「差不多能 work、又处在边缘」的东西，因为一旦模型到位，你会远远领先于所有人。好。最后一个问题。你刚才说的也许已经回答了，但什么让你夜不能寐？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: The thing that keeps me up at night is probably... It's how we... So we talked about Claude Code and Cowork team culture and the team culture is really important to me. It's the one team mentality and I share with folks. And by the way, culture is like a living, breathing thing. It's not just a poster you slap on a wall and it changes over time and it shows up in how we treat each other, how we're there for each other. And so the culture of the team is important to me because we are growing and since the culture shifts, making sure that maintaining the things are important, that we still really... It's really important for me to have diverse perspectives so then we can have good, healthy, open, honest, debates out in the open and we welcome those and what I call that one team mentality that when you get close to the finish line, look behind you and see is there some teams to help because we finish as a team. (01:19:02): That's probably the thing that keeps me up at night. There's so many other hard problems, right? But I think maybe a lot of the other ones are product or engineering challenges that yes, we have dashboards or theories or hypothesis, but the culture is like a human aspect that is... I think that's the one that I always want to make sure that we're as we grow, we're still maintaining that culture because it is the fiber of the team. And when it starts drifting... I'm always worried if it drifts, are we catching it and having conversations as a team together to make sure we're all wanting the culture to grow in the right direction?
turns.zh: 让我夜不能寐的，大概是……就是我们聊过的 Claude Code 和 Cowork 的团队文化，团队文化对我极重要。是那种「一个团队（one team）」的心态，我跟大伙分享的。顺便说，文化是个会呼吸、活着的 thing。它不是你拍在墙上的一张海报，它会随时间变，它体现在我们怎么对待彼此、怎么彼此支持。所以团队的文化对我重要，因为我们在成长，而既然文化在漂移，确保我们维护那些重要的东西——我们真的……对我来说极重要的是有多元的视角，这样我们才能有健康、开放、诚实的辩论，把这些摊开来，我们欢迎这些，以及我说的那种「一个团队」心态：当你接近终点线时，回头看看身后有没有哪个团队需要帮忙，因为我们是作为一个团队冲线的。(01:19:02)：那大概就是让我夜不能寐的东西。还有那么多别的硬问题，对吧？但我想也许很多其他的都是产品或工程挑战——对，我们有看板、有理论、有假设，但文化是种人的面向，它……我想那是我永远想确保的：随着我们成长，我们还在维护那种文化，因为它是团队的生命纤维。而当它开始漂移……我总担心，如果它漂移了，我们有没有 catch 到、并作为团队一起去对话，确保我们都希望文化朝对的方向长？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I imagine everybody is struggling with this considering the pace of change and the phase of hiring, just like... Especially at a company like Anthropic that's in this crazy, the most unprecedented growth trajectory in history. I could see how that could be a challenge with so much change. So it makes sense. Even at Airbnb when I was there, that was quite a growth trajectory and that was nothing like what you guys are going through and that was a constant topic of conversation. How do we maintain the culture?
turns.zh: 对。我想在变化的速度和招聘的阶段下，大家应该都在跟这个挣扎——尤其像 Anthropic 这样的公司，处在史上 unprecedented 的增长轨迹里。我能想象那在这么多变化下会是个挑战。所以这讲得通。哪怕在我待过的 Airbnb，那也是条相当猛的增长轨迹，但跟你正在经历的完全不是一个量级，而那是个一直被聊的话题：我们怎么维护文化？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Actually, I'm curious, what was your experience at BAB to maintain the culture as we're growing?
turns.zh: 其实我好奇，你在 BAB（Airbnb）维护文化的经验是怎样的，随着我们成长？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a couple of things. One is just what worked well is the founders being obsessed with it. Every all hands, every big meeting is just reminding of the culture and the value of the culture and what the values are. Just the founders top down being obsessed with it was a big part of it. You just couldn't have a meeting without that coming up as a thing. The other is a memory I always come back to is we had Cheryl Sandberg's PKMETA come do a fireside chat and somebody asked her just, how do you maintain culture as you scale? Because we're just growing so fast and it's so hard to deal with all this change and culture and all these new people. And her advice was, "This is actually a problem you want to have because this means you're growing and doing well and this is normal versus nothing will change if you're doing badly." (01:21:18): That's a much worse situation when you're not growing and you're not hiring like crazy. That's a much worse situation that will cause even more pain and suffering. So this is a good problem you're dealing with is her advice, which has always stuck with me.
turns.zh: 有几件事。一件是 work 得好的：创始人 obsession 于它。每次全员会、每次大会议，都在提醒文化、文化的价值、价值观是什么。就是创始人自上而下地 obsession 于它，那是很大一部分。你根本开不了一次没有它冒出来的会。另一件是我总回到的一段记忆：我们请了 Cheryl Sandberg 的 PKMETA 来做 fireside chat（炉边谈话），有人问她：随着规模化，你怎么维护文化？因为我们成长太快了，要应对所有这些变化、文化、还有这么多新人，太难了。而她的建议是：「这其实是你想要的问题，因为这意味着你在成长、做得好；相比之下，如果你做得差，什么都不会变。」(01:21:18)：那是个糟糕得多的处境——当你不成长、不疯狂招人时。那才是会导致更多痛苦和折磨的更糟处境。所以「这是你正在应对的一个好问题」是她的建议，而那一直留在我心里。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Oh, that's great. It's interesting hearing you talk, I think one of the important things to Claude Code and Cowork team is whether ICs or managers, but this is a thing I especially as for managers on the team is really important that we all talk about for sure what's going out, but also just be open about what's not going well because then if we can actually have a conversation of what's not going well, that's how we can actually go ahead and address it. Speaking of what keeps me up in that, my nightmare is, especially if someone's in a manager position and I'm like, "Hey, how are things going? Everything's fine." I'm like, "Oh, my gosh, I'm not doing fine. I know this thing's..." You know how there was this meme of the dog drinking a cup of coffee in a room that's on fire? That is my nightmare. (01:22:17): So that's actually a discussion I have with a lot of folks on the team by special managers, especially when they first join up, "Hey, let's always have these open conversations so that we can solve problems together."
turns.zh: 哦，那太棒了。听你聊很有意思，我想 Claude Code 和 Cowork 团队里一件重要的事是——无论 IC 还是经理——但我特别想说，对团队里的经理，有件事极重要：我们当然都聊什么在顺利推出，但也要对「什么不顺利」保持开放，因为如果我们能真正开一场「什么不顺利」的对话，那才是我们真能往前去解决它的方式。说到让我夜不能寐的，我的噩梦是——尤其如果某人处在经理位置，而我在想：「嘿，事情怎么样？都挺好。」我就在想：「哦我的天，我可一点都不好。我知道这事儿……」你记得那个 meme 吗——一只狗在着火的房间里喝咖啡？那就是我的噩梦。(01:22:17)：所以那其实是我跟团队很多人、尤其经理们——尤其他们刚加入时——的一场对话：「嘿，咱们永远保持这些开放的对话，这样我们才能一起解决问题。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine this is something a lot of people struggle with seeing so many people around them doing super well, at least seemingly doing well, everything's going great, I'm growing, this awesome company or just like everything, it's like hard to actually be honest and say, "It's not going great. I'm struggling here. I'm falling behind," because everyone around you is just like on the surface feeling like they're killing it. (01:22:53): Before we get to our very exciting lightning round, is there anything else that you either want to leave listeners with, anything else that we didn't cover? Anything else that's important that you wanted to share?
turns.zh: 我想这是很多人都在挣扎的事——看到身边那么多人做得超好，至少表面上是超好、一切顺利、我在成长、这家超棒的公司、或者就一切——真的很难诚实地说：「其实不怎么顺利。我这儿在挣扎。我在落后。」因为你身边每个人都表面上看像在杀疯了。(01:22:53)：在我们进入超刺激的闪电轮之前，还有没有别的——你想留给听众的、我们没覆盖到的？还有什么是你想分享的重要东西？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Maybe one thing is just a suggestion because we talked about how can Claude do automate. One other thing that's really big on Claude Code and Cowork team culture is explicit permission to kill processes that no longer serve us. And so maybe a suggestion is for anyone working on a team or leading teams, what's one process that you either dread doing or is really highly noisy or is really expensive in terms of just a lot of... Or something that's just very manual, pick one thing and first ask is it still having its purpose? For example, when even our planning... Actually, that was my own big first learning when I first joined Claude Code. I'm like, "Hey, maybe we should do a six-month roadmap doc, but we're going to do it super lightweight because I don't want to waste a lot of time planning." And I felt we did a really lightweight process, but that was such a good learning for me because the exercise was good to kickstart conversations and enter aligned, but three months into it, I'm like, "Wait, have we still referenced stuff?" Because so much has changed. (01:24:10): So that was also something I... And so that was also something I changed that I myself brought in thinking, "Hey, maybe this will help." So always be open to learning and always ask yourself whatever process you have, is it still serving its purpose just because the field is changing so fast?
turns.zh: 也许一件事就是个建议，因为我们聊了 Claude 怎么能自动化。另一件在 Claude Code 和 Cowork 团队文化里特别大的是：明确授权去 kill 那些不再服务我们的流程。所以也许一个建议是：对任何在团队里工作或带团队的人——有什么流程是你要么害怕做、要么极吵、要么极贵（就那种大把……）的？或者什么东西极手动，挑一件，先问：它还有它的目的吗？比如，连我们的规划……其实那是我刚加入 Claude Code 时自己的第一个大学习。我在想：「嘿，也许我们该做个六个月路线图文档，但我们要做得超轻量，因为我不想浪费大把时间规划。」而我觉得我们做了个超轻量的流程，但那对我是个极好的学习——因为那个练习很好、能 kickstart 对话、让我们对齐，但三个月进去后，我在想：「等等，我们还有在引用那些东西吗？」因为变化太大了。(01:24:10)：所以那也是我……所以我改了那件事，是我自己带进来的、想着「嘿，也许这会有帮助」。所以永远对 learning 保持开放，永远问自己：你有的任何流程，它还在服务它的目的吗？只因为这个领域变得太快了？

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 我爱那个建议。我得就这个快速追一下。你现在怎么看规划？你还做规划吗？是只做一个月的路线图吗？用最简单的方式解释一下你现在的状况？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yeah, I call it JIT planning now, just in time planning. So it is around, because yeah, I think six months was too long. So now for sure some projects will take more than a month, but we try to do a month planning, really lightweight. Actually, there's not even dogs. It's really just us aligning on a little spreadsheet of what we think is important. But even that one, I'm thinking through, hey, every week we should probably still keep what we're trying is here are the month's priorities and we're going to try it out, but I have a feeling like every week we'll probably want to do really quick like, "Hey, just to check, yep, this is still this month's priorities, good." But now we've shrunk it to JIT monthly planning.
turns.zh: 对，我现在叫它 JIT 规划（just in time，准时制规划）。所以是围绕——对，我想六个月太长了。所以现在当然有些项目会超过一个月，但我们试着做一个月的规划，真的超轻量。其实连文档都没有。真的就我们在个小表格里对齐「我们认为重要的东西」。但连那个，我也在想：嘿，每周我们大概还是该留着「我们在试的是这个——这是本月的优先级，我们要试试」，但我有种感觉，每周我们大概想做个超快的：「嘿，确认一下，对，这还是本月优先级，好。」但现在我们把它缩到了 JIT 月度规划。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it's monthly meaning for the next month, here's a little sheet/Excel spreadsheet of what we're planning to do for the next month and then every week check-in is this still what we're planning to do for the next month?
turns.zh: 所以是 monthly——意思是下个月，这是张小表格/Excel，列着我们计划下个月做的事，然后每周 check-in：这还是我们计划下个月做的吗？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So cool.
turns.zh: 太酷了。

turns.en: Very, very weird. But even that one, I'm also still feeling, how can we even automate this more? Because I never want it to be feeling like attacked when someone has to update the spreadsheet. So this is actually, just yesterday we're chatting, "Hey, how can we actually automate this?" Speaking to that question, always ask yourselves, "Can we actually automate this better?"
turns.zh: 非常、非常怪。但连那个，我也还在想：我们怎么把它更自动化？因为我永远不想让某人在不得不更新表格时感觉像被攻击。所以这其实——就在昨天我们在聊：「嘿，我们怎么真正自动化这个？」顺着那个问题，永远问自己：「我们能把它自动化得更好吗？」

turns.en: My PM brain is like, "How could you not do something like that? Okay, here's what we're thinking for the next month. Let's just check it once a week, make sure this is..." turns.zh: 我那个 PM 脑子就像：「你怎么能不做那样的事？好，这是我们对下个月的想法。咱们一周查一次，确保这是……」很难想象这不发生、而且你这张表格上没多少条——这也是我听到的。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Yeah, we really try focus. So we'll share, here's what we think are the highest priorities. And again, for that agency, given the priorities, then everybody's their kind of item for how they think addresses those priorities.
turns.zh: 对，我们真的试着聚焦。所以我们会分享：这是我们认为的最高优先级。而再说一次，为了那个 agency，给定了优先级，然后每个人都有自己那一条——关于他们觉得怎么去应对那些优先级。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung

turns.zh: 所以通常绝对有我们认为工作所在的主题。其实整个团队每六个月会把所有人聚一起。所以通常会 kick off 一些主题，但然后真的是确保我们保持对……pulse 的把握，因为再说一次，连那些主题在环境一变时也变得太快。

turns.zh: 好，咱们把表格拉出来。咱们看看。哦天呐，天呐，这整期播客本来可以就聊你做的这个规划。好。我得找别人来聊这个，因为这太有意思了——你们到底怎么规划。对。好。那么 Fiona，说到这，我们到了超刺激的闪电轮。我有五个问题给你。准备好了吗？

turns.en: Ready.

turns.en: Okay. First question, what are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?

turns.en: Ooh, I will say for fiction, actually two authors I recommend to everyone, Margaret Atwood and Haruki Murakami. I mean, I grew up in Canada, so I read a lot of that when growing up, but her books are fascinating because it's almost like speculative fiction of you can squint and say, "Okay, could this actually happen to a society?" So I love her take on speculative fiction and Murakami, I love his magical realism style. But then the one book, so there are authors, but the one book I always recommend to everyone to read at least once a year, The Little Prince, I'm sure we probably all read it at some point in our lives, but I think I read it at least once a year just to remind me to think about what's truly important.
turns.zh: 哦，我会说虚构类——其实我推荐给每个人的两位作者：Margaret Atwood 和 Haruki Murakami（村上春树）。我是说，我在加拿大长大，所以成长中读了很多那个，但她的书迷人，因为它几乎是推想小说（speculative fiction）——你眯眼一看会说：「好吧，这真能在社会里发生吗？」所以我爱她对推想小说的处理；而 Murakami，我爱他的魔幻现实主义风格。但然后有本书——所以是作者，但我总会推荐给每个人、每年至少读一次的，是《小王子》（The Little Prince），我想我们人生里某刻大概都读过，但我想我每年至少读一次，就为了提醒自己去思考什么才是真正重要的。

(01:29:18): And the other two are Ghibli films. I love Spirited Away. I just love that story. I just love everything about Spirited Away. It's probably one of my favorite Ghibli films. turns.zh: 但我会跟你分享我手机里一直下好的——这样如果我在飞机上……所以有三部电影我会一直放手机里，因为我想它们真的好看、有时间就看。一部是 Emily。是部法国电影，哦我的天，所有这些电影都会很老，顺便说。会是那种 vintage 电影，但我爱 Emily，超 whimsical（异想天开）。所以真的强烈推荐给没看过的任何人。如果你记得，我跟你说过我要去一趟……我以为我要当视觉艺术家。所以 16 岁那会儿，我高中组织了趟巴黎的旅行，关于那次我有太多记忆了，而 Emily 真的捕捉到了我在巴黎感受到的魔力。(01:29:18)：另外两部是 Ghibli（吉卜力）电影。我爱《千与千寻》（Spirited Away）。我就是爱那个故事。我对《千与千寻》的一切都爱。它大概是我最爱的吉卜力电影之一。然后第三部是另一部吉卜力电影，《风之谷》（Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind）。我对这部想得相当多，因为如果有人问我：「嘿，你怎么想出所有这些领导力特质的？」我想我大概八九岁时看了那部电影，而女主角 Nausicaä 以及看她怎么领导，在我心里留下了印章——你大概能这么说——也许 Nausicaä 在很多我的不同领导力原则上都启发了我。

turns.en: I'll share the product that I'm reminded of how much has made a difference in my life recently because I've been just traveling a little bit and I like to travel really light so I use whatever shampoo and conditioner the hotel gives and I forgot that... So the product that I actually have one of their hand, I promise is it's not an infomercial, but Sweet Sisters Body Care, it's a local business on Whidbey Island, but the reason why their product has made such a big difference in my life, it's a full line of organic, hair, body, skincare. But a few years ago, I started getting this rash on my nose right here that was really painful, actually bleeding. And I could not for the life of me figure out how to stop it. I tried not using any lotions. I cut everything on my face and it was still really hurting. And then somebody says, "What's the shampoo you're using?" I'm like, "It's the same shampoo I've used since I was a teenager." And they're like, "Maybe your body has now..." And it's like generic brand shampoo they get anywhere. (01:31:39): And they said, "May your bodies just start developing an allergy to it because of the chemicals in it that..." I'm like, "What?" And so anyways, this was an organic shampoo that I found. Lo and behold, I use our shampoo because you don't think that when you wash your hair, it actually then goes over to the rest of your body. So since then, I've switched everything that I used to be Sweet Sisters, but I'm recently reminded of how important this is because after a week of hotel shampoo, I actually started having some skin reactions again. I'm like, "Ah, maybe I should get travel size bottles that I could bring with me."
turns.zh: 我会分享那个让我最近被提醒「它给我的生活带来了多大不同」的产品，因为我最近出了点差，而我喜欢特别轻装旅行，所以用酒店给的任何洗发水护发素——我忘了那个……所以其实我手头有一家的产品，我保证这不是 infomercial（电视购物广告），但 Sweet Sisters Body Care，是 Whidbey Island 上的一家本地生意；而他们的产品给我的生活带来这么大不同的原因是：它是一整条有机的头发、身体、护肤线。但几年前，我开始鼻子这儿长一种疹子，真的痛，还会流血。我死活想不出怎么让它停。我试过不用任何乳液。我把脸上一切全停了，它还是好痛。然后有人说：「你用的什么洗发水？」我说：「就是我青少年起一直用的同款。」他们说：「也许你的身体现在……」而那是随便哪都能买到的 generic 品牌洗发水。(01:31:39)：他们说：「也许你的身体开始对它过敏了，因为里面的化学物质……」我说：「什么？」总之，这是我找到的一款有机洗发水。你瞧，我用我们的洗发水——因为你不会想到，你洗头发时，它其实会流到身体其他部位。所以从那以后，我把所有东西都换成了 Sweet Sisters，但我最近被提醒这有多重要，因为用了一周酒店洗发水后，我其实又开始有些皮肤反应了。我在想：「啊，也许我该弄点旅行装瓶子随身带着。」

turns.zh: 这是个超棒的选。我爱本地生意的选，光这点就加分。顺便说，你这趟旅行——给可能不知道的人——有个 Code with Claude 活动正在世界各地办。我去了 SF 那场，伦敦有一场，你要去东京那场。那是终点还是之后还有更多？

turns.en: Tokyo is... So yeah, that's next week and that's the last leg of the trip.

turns.zh: 好。那以后大概还会有更多。太酷了。我爱这个在发生。好，还有两个问题。你有没有一句常回到的、在工作或生活里的人生格言？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Ooh. So in work, I really love to remind folks, keep it simple. What is the thing that you're really trying to do well and focus on that? Keep it simple because I think sometimes we could overthink. So it's always a good mantra to think about that. And then in life, probably in a world where you can be anything, be kind.
turns.zh: 哦。工作上，我超爱提醒大伙：保持简单（keep it simple）。你真正想做好的事是什么、就聚焦在那上面？保持简单，因为我想有时我们会 overthinking。所以那永远是个好 mantra 去想的。然后生活上，大概是在「你可以成为任何东西」的世界里，be kind（善良）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that one. We were at a Montessori school tour and that's what the teacher had up on the wall.
turns.zh: 我爱那句。我们当时在一个蒙特梭利学校的参观里，那正是老师贴在墙上的话。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: We have so many things going on that you never know what's going on in someone else's life and that one small act of kindness can make the biggest difference. For me actually that was when... Do you remember COVID? We were all working from home during the COVID-
turns.zh: 我们有太多事在发生，你永远不知道别人生活里在经历什么，而那一个小小的善意举动，能造成最大的不同。对我而言其实那是当……你记得 COVID 吗？我们那会儿都居家办公——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How could I forget?
turns.zh: 我怎么能忘？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: It's just always really struck with me because I was in these back to back meetings and one-on-ones are really important to me because actually that time is usually also really important for the other person. It's something that they've been looking to. They might have things discussed. I always really prioritize one-on-ones, but during that time, my grandmother wasn't doing well and she was in a home in Canada because of COVID I couldn't go visit and actually even my aunt and mom couldn't go visit and it was just very rare of if they have a helper that can help, we could do FaceTime, but you never know what time that is going to be because there's so many people that take care and all of a sudden I get a message from my aunt going, "Grandma can FaceTime at 12:00 PM today." I'm like, "Oh, no, there's this one-on-one that I've been mean to have." And I just messaged my report to say, "I'm really, really sorry. It's the last minute. Is it okay to..." (01:34:36): And I know now when I say it doesn't seem like it's a big thing because it's like... But to me, it's always really important to keep. But he was like, "Yeah, totally. No problem at all." And for me, that was just a small after kindness and he totally didn't make it into big deal, but that made the biggest difference to me that I got to say hi to my grandmother on FaceTime.
turns.zh: 它一直真的戳中我，因为我当时一个接一个会。而一对一（one-on-one）对我极重要，因为其实那段时光对对方通常也极重要。是他们一直在盼着的事。他们可能有事要讨论。我永远把一对一排最高优先级，但在那段时间，我奶奶身体不好，她在加拿大的一家养老院，因为 COVID 我没法去探望，其实连我阿姨和妈妈都没法去探望，而能有个帮手帮着、我们才能 FaceTime 的情况极少——你永远不知道那会是什么时候，因为有太多照顾她的人。突然我阿姨给我发消息：「奶奶今天中午 12 点能 FaceTime。」我在想：「哦不，有个我本该有的一对一。」而我只是给我那个下属发消息说：「我真的、真的很抱歉。太临时了。能不能……」(01:34:36)：而我知道现在我说起来好像不是什么大事——但对我而言，保持那个永远极重要。而他就说：「对，完全没问题。一点事都没有。」而对我而言，那就是一个小小的善意——他完全没把它当回事，但那对我造成了最大的不同，让我能在 FaceTime 上跟我奶奶问声好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Okay, final question. So Boris Chernyy, when I asked him about you, when he had this interesting insight where he said in very important meetings, you can often hear Fiona, you can hear the click-clack of Fiona knitting in the background. Maybe talk about just what's going on there and what are a couple of things you knitted recently.
turns.zh: 我爱那个。好，最后一个问题。我问 Boris Cherny 关于你时，他有个有意思的洞察：在很重要的会议里，你常常能听到 Fiona，能听到背景里 Fiona 织毛衣的「click-clack」声。也许聊聊那是在干嘛，以及你最近织了哪几件？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Oh, my gosh. Well, I knitted this top recently.
turns.zh: 哦我的天。嗯，我最近织了这件上衣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You make your own clothing. Unreal. This is very meta for Claude Code building itself.
turns.zh: 你自己做衣服。不真实。这对 Claude Code 构建它自己来说太 meta 了。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Actually, there's this whole fun thing I think between knitting and programming because it's like two stitches knit and a pearl. So zero and one. And anyway, so many concepts of stacks and queues you actually could... I'm kind of a compiler. I'm kind of generating an executable when I knit. Yeah, actually it was my grandma that taught me to knit when I was eight. I mentioned her and I going to that yarn shop. And so every time I knit, I think of her, but I always like to multitask as you could see like, yeah, kick off multiple agents. And so anytime I'm sitting and because I practice enough and got proficient at it, I don't have to look at what I'm doing. So it's almost like how you know sometimes people have like fidget spinners and such. Knitting is just... So anytime I'm sitting still, I'm like, "Oh, this is time to generate more knitting executable." Because I got so much yarn that if I don't do this, I might have a slight yarn addiction problem.
turns.zh: 其实，织毛衣和编程之间有个整个好玩的联系，因为它就像两针：knit（平针）和 pearl（反针）。也就是 0 和 1。总之，很多 stacks 和 queues 的概念你其实能……我有点像个编译器。我织的时候有点像在生成一个可执行文件。对，其实是我奶奶八岁时教我织的。我提到过她和我去那家毛线店。所以每次我织，我都会想到她，但我总喜欢 multitask——就像你能看到的，对，kick off 多个 agent。所以任何时候我坐着——因为我练得够多、已经熟练了，我不用看我在干嘛。所以它几乎就像有些人有 fidget spinner（指尖陀螺）之类。织毛衣就是……所以任何时候我坐着不动，我就在想：「哦，这是生成更多织毛衣可执行文件的时间。」因为我囤了这么多毛线，如果我不织，我可能有轻微的毛线成瘾问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this. When I asked Boris what he would do when AGI hits, when we don't have to work, he said he's going to make me so... I'm guessing your answer would be just knit and make beautiful clothing.
turns.zh: 我爱这个。我问 Boris 当 AGI 降临、我们不用工作时他会干嘛，他说他要把我……我猜你的答案会是就织毛衣、做漂亮衣服。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Oh, my gosh. My dream is to actually open up a yarn store in my grandmother's name-
turns.zh: 哦我的天。我的梦想其实是开一家以我奶奶命名的毛线店——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There we go.
turns.zh: 这就对了。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: ...and create that community.
turns.zh: ……并创造那种社区。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow. And then Cowork would help out you automate everything.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。而然后 Cowork 会帮你把一切自动化。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: That's great. Especially invoicing.
turns.zh: 那太棒了。尤其开发票。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, my God. Fiona, you're awesome. It's just incredible the work that you and your team are doing, just changing the world in such profound ways and it's clear why it's growing so fast. So good job. Good job over there. (01:37:04): Thank you for making time for this.
turns.zh: 哦我的天。Fiona，你太牛了。你和你的团队在做的工作就是不可思议，以这么深远的影响改变世界，而且很清楚为什么它成长得这么快。所以干得好。那边干得好。(01:37:04)：谢谢你抽时间做这期。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Well, I'm just really honestly lucky and humble that I get to work with such an amazing team. I know how lucky I am and I'm so grateful. But thanks a lot for having me on the podcast as well. This was a lot of fun.
turns.zh: 嗯，我只是真的又幸运又谦卑，能跟这么棒的团队合作。我知道我多幸运，我无比感恩。但也超感谢你让我上这播客。这太好玩了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if you are online if they want to follow up on anything and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 最后两个问题。如果大家想在线上找到你、想跟进任何事，去哪找？以及听众能怎么帮到你？

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Ooh, so definitely I'm on LinkedIn and I'm sure most people have shared this already, but would love feedback of what's going well, what's not going well, also any latent demand that you are all using that might be interesting use cases. I had a friend message me recently to go, "Oh, I'm using Claude to help me generate a building plan for my shed." And he actually showed me his whole shed, which was cool. So would love to hear about that. And then yeah, maybe also we talked about reaching out across. So there's someone, whether a small business that you love or someone that you feel like hasn't... As all the listeners are super AI pilled, maybe take a time to hold somebody's hand to show what AI might be able to help them with.
turns.zh: 哦，我绝对在 LinkedIn 上，而且我猜大多数人都已经分享过了，但我想要关于「什么顺利、什么不顺利」的反馈，也包括任何你们在用、可能是有意思用例的潜在需求。我最近有个朋友给我发消息说：「哦，我在用 Claude 帮我生成我那个棚屋（shed）的建造计划。」他还给我看了他整个棚屋，挺酷的。所以会很想听到那些。然后对，也许我们也聊过跨出去去联系。所以无论谁——一家你爱的本地小生意，或者你觉得还没……既然所有听众都被 AI 武装得很彻底，也许花点时间牵着某人的手，展示 AI 可能怎么帮到他们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a good one. That is such a good answer to this question, especially coming from you. Fiona, this was awesome. Thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太好的一个。那是对这个问题太好的一个回答，尤其出自你之口。Fiona，这期太棒了。太感谢你来了。

turns.speaker: Fiona Fung
turns.en: Thanks so much for having me, Lenny.
turns.zh: Lenny，太感谢你邀请我。
